metadata.title: The Management Of Angle-Closure Glaucoma
metadata.summary: This guideline addresses diagnosis, referral, treatment and follow-up across the primary angle-closure spectrum, from suspected disease to acute crises and established glaucoma. It evaluates preventive treatment, lens extraction, laser procedures, medication and glaucoma surgery, including management considerations for cataract and small eyes. Secondary angle-closure disease is outside its stated scope, although secondary mechanisms are discussed where distinguishing them changes acute care.

target_population: People with suspected or established primary angle-closure disease
People presenting with an acute angle-closure crisis
First-degree relatives of people with significant primary angle-closure disease
People with cataract and angle-closure disease
therapeutic_areas: medical treatment to lower intraocular pressure

prevention: Studies have not consistently shown that iridotomy location changes dysphotopsia risk; a PI may be placed superiorly (12 o’clock) or temporally.
Anti-coagulants need not be stopped for PI when INR < 3.

toxicities.event: Aggravation of lenticular or retro-lenticular angle-closure by pilocarpine
recognition: Marked asymmetry of central anterior chamber depth may indicate a lenticular or retro-lenticular mechanism.
An affected patient may have persistent pain and delayed control of intraocular pressure if treated with pilocarpine.

management.severity: Acute symptoms or high intraocular pressure
management.actions: Use pupil dilation with atropine +/- phenylephrine rather than pilocarpine; cyclopentolate is also identified as an effective initial treatment for lenticular or retro-lenticular block.

prevention: Identify secondary lenticular and retro-lenticular mechanisms before giving pilocarpine.
In the acute care pathway, substitute Atropine 1% for G. Pilocarpine 2%* when the cause is lenticular or retro-lenticular.

toxicities.event: Drug allergies or serious side-effects relevant to systemic acetazolamide
recognition: History of allergy to sulphonamide medications such trimethoprim
prevention: Before initial systemic acetazolamide treatment, promptly check for relevant allergies and severe nephropathy.
Do not prescribe the stated post-dilation PO acetazolamide regimen when its use is contraindicated.

toxicities.event: Acute angle-closure associated with pharmacological pupil dilation
toxicities.incidence: Between 1/5,000 and 1/10,000 during routine eye examinations across the general adult population.
recognition: Sudden reduction or loss of vision
prevention: Routine dilation remains appropriate for most patients because the risk is very low.

For established or probable angle-closure, dilation can generally be performed with tropicamide alone, followed by PO acetazolamide 250mg on leaving the department and another dose at bedtime that night, unless contraindicated.
Do not use pilocarpine to constrict the pupil after dilation: it may hold the pupil partly dilated and increase angle-closure risk.
For patients needing repeated dilation, particularly for diabetic retinopathy screening, consider specialist assessment for prophylactic laser iridotomy.

recognition: topiramate may cause supraciliary effusions and anterior rotation of the ciliary body; associated posterior-segment angle-closure can present bilaterally.
Use of antidepressant medication (SSRI and tricyclics) is associated with increased angle-closure risk.

management.severity: Suspected atypical angle-closure associated with topiramate
management.actions: Ask directly about topiramate use. Discuss the possibility of an alternative medication with the prescribing physician; direct care toward the underlying drug-associated pathology.

prevention: Advise patients taking antidepressant medication (SSRI and tricyclics) about the increased risk and to discuss their need for the medication with its prescriber.

toxicities.event: Complications of lens or cataract surgery in nanophthalmos
toxicities.incidence: Complications may occur in 30% of cases or more in patients with nanophthalmos. In patients with shorter axial length, the complication rate doubles with every 1 mm short axial length below 21mm.
prevention: Counsel patients with nanophthalmos about surgical complications and the possibility of a refractive surprise because accurate biometry is difficult.
For axial length < 21.00, explain and document the excess surgical risk.
When extracting a lens in nanophthalmos, consider surgical iridectomy during the operation to reduce postoperative pupil block and facilitate management should aqueous misdirection occur.
In very small eyes with very shallow anterior chambers, consider concurrent pars plana vitrectomy after discussion with a vitreo-retinal surgeon.

toxicities.incidence: In a small RCT of medically uncontrolled PACG eyes with clear lens, surgical complications occurred in 44% of the trabeculectomy group versus 4% of the phacoemulsification group. One third of patients undergoing trabeculectomy developed significant cataract within 2 years. Studies in PACG with coexisting cataract reported more complications with phacotrabeculectomy than with phacoemulsification alone, without a stated rate.
prevention: Suggested trabeculectomy modifications in PACG include a more anterior sclerostomy and maintenance of a deep anterior chamber, with sutures placed before sclerostomy to avoid extreme intraoperative intraocular-pressure fluctuations.
Suggested measures against post-operative hypotony include multiple tight scleral-flap sutures, conservative suture lysis or removal, and cycloplegic therapy.

recognition: Sudden shallowing of the anterior chamber, especially after an operation
Intraocular pressure that may be normal
Risk factors include short axial length, an angle-closure diagnosis and being phakic.

management.actions: Use atropine or cyclopentolate with systemic and/or topical aqueous-production suppressants, followed by a hyperosmotic such as mannitol if not contraindicated. Perform a peripheral iridotomy if a patent one is not already present.

Phakic eyes may require pars plana vitrectomy with or without lens extraction. In pseudophakic eyes, Nd:YAG laser vitreolysis/capsulotomy may be tried. Zonulo-hyaloido-vitrectomy through an anterior-chamber approach or a pars plana approach is another option; diode laser cyclophotocoagulation is an effective alternative in many cases.

prevention: Good evidence to guide prevention is lacking. In nanophthalmos undergoing lens or cataract extraction, consider surgical iridectomy to help manage aqueous misdirection if it develops.

toxicities.event: Severe complications associated with limbal paracentesis
prevention: Paracentesis has no proven role in acute angle-closure management and may cause harm; reports of severe complications are anecdotal.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Laser PI is advised for PACS PLUS when additional risk factors are present.
prophylaxis.target_population: People with PACS PLUS, including those with an only good eye, vulnerable adults who may not report symptoms, a family history of significant angle-closure disease, high hypermetropia (> + 6.00 dioptres), diabetes or another condition requiring regular pupil dilation, use of antidepressants or medication with an anticholinergic action, or residence or work where rapid emergency ophthalmic care is unavailable.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Perform laser iridotomy promptly in the contralateral eye when an acute symptomatic attack has occurred; attempt it before discharge once intraocular pressure is controlled.
prophylaxis.target_population: Contralateral fellow eyes of patients with acute angle-closure
prophylaxis.duration: At the time when the acute angle-closure is treated, before discharge once intraocular pressure is controlled.

prophylaxis.recommendation: First-degree relatives should receive regular community optometric reviews and, if current referral criteria are met, be referred to hospital eye services for consideration of prophylactic laser iridotomy.
prophylaxis.target_population: First-degree relatives of patients with significant primary angle-closure disease, excluding relatives referred solely because the patient is a primary angle-closure suspect

prophylaxis.recommendation: For patients at risk during repeated dilation for diabetic retinopathy screening, consider glaucoma specialist review to assess prophylactic laser iridotomy.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with diabetes who need repeated pupil dilation and are at risk of angle-closure

prophylaxis.recommendation: Consider surgical iridectomy during lens or cataract extraction to reduce postoperative pupil block and facilitate treatment if aqueous misdirection occurs.
prophylaxis.target_population: Eyes with nanophthalmos undergoing lens or cataract extraction

therapies_index.name: laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI)
therapies_index.mechanism: Creates an opening that can relieve obstruction to aqueous circulation associated with pupil block.
approved_indications: Advised for PACS PLUS when additional risk factors are present; not advised routinely for PACS without additional risk factors.
Recommended promptly for acute angle-closure and for the contralateral eye when an acute symptomatic attack has occurred.
May help control earlier stages of angle-closure associated with pupil block; its use may be considered even when a non-pupil-block mechanism is suspected.
A patent peripheral iridotomy is required in aqueous misdirection if one is not already present.
therapies_index.administration: For acute angle-closure, perform as soon as technically feasible; treat both eyes after the initial attack resolves. Attempt treatment of the fellow eye without delay, before discharge, once IOP is controlled.
key_toxicities: Dysphotopsia may occur; studies have not consistently linked its frequency to iridotomy location.
Bleeding is discussed in relation to the procedure.
monitoring: Gonioscopy can assess residual iridotrabecular contact; AS OCT can document changes in angle width before and after treatment.

therapies_index.name: sequential argon/YAG PI
approved_indications: Preferred for dark irides, including those of people of Asian or African descent.

therapies_index.name: surgical iridectomy
approved_indications: May be attempted in both eyes after resolution of an initial acute angle-closure attack.
May be considered during lens or cataract extraction in nanophthalmos to reduce postoperative pupil block and facilitate management if aqueous misdirection occurs.
therapies_index.administration: For nanophthalmos, consider performing it at the time of lens or cataract extraction.

therapies_index.name: clear lens extraction (CLE)
therapies_index.mechanism: Removing the lens helps relieve barriers to aqueous circulation within the eye.
approved_indications: Can be considered initially for mild to moderate PACG and for PAC with IOP > 30 mmHg in patients over 50 years of age.
Clear lens phaco is advised as the primary intervention for PACG.
therapies_index.administration: Decisions to extract the lens for angle-closure control should involve a consultant with a specialist interest in glaucoma.
key_toxicities: Lens extraction in angle-closure can be more complicated during and after surgery than in routine eyes.
monitoring: IOP and subsequent need for glaucoma medication or surgery.

therapies_index.name: phacoemulsification
therapies_index.mechanism: Lens removal can improve aqueous drainage in angle-closure disease.
approved_indications: Preferred over laser PI for PAC with IOP > 30mmHg.
Initial treatment option for early to moderate PACG with co-existing cataract.
Early treatment should be offered after acute angle-closure in patients with cataract once IOP is controlled and the cornea is clear.
therapies_index.administration: For acute angle-closure with cataract, offer approximately 1 to 4 weeks after presentation once IOP is controlled and the cornea is clear.
key_toxicities: The complication rate doubles with every 1 mm short axial length below 21mm.
monitoring: Consider the accuracy of ocular biometry and the likely refractive outcome in very small eyes.

therapies_index.name: phaco/IOL
approved_indications: A cited trial studied phacoemulsification with an intraocular lens implant after AAC in patients whose IOP reached ≤30 mmHg within 24 hours with medical treatment and who had cataract with visual acuity of ≤6/15.
therapies_index.administration: The cited trial performed treatment within 1 week of presentation.

therapies_index.name: goniosynechialysis (GSL)
therapies_index.administration: Studied as an addition to phacoemulsification; the guideline advises against carrying it out because a larger randomised trial found no additional benefit.

therapies_index.name: trabeculectomy
approved_indications: May be considered for severe PACG.
Trabeculectomy with mitomycin-C may be indicated for medically uncontrolled PACG without cataract, particularly in younger patients with accommodative ability.
Primary trabeculectomy with mitomycin-C may be an option in advanced PACG with uncontrolled IOP and concurrent cataract.
Emergency trabeculectomy is not advised for an acute angle-closure attack.
therapies_index.administration: Suggested modifications in PACG include a more anterior sclerostomy, maintenance of a deep anterior chamber, sutures placed before sclerostomy, multiple tight scleral-flap sutures, cautious suture lysis or removal, and cycloplegic therapy.
key_toxicities: In a cited trial of medically uncontrolled PACG with a clear lens, surgical complications occurred in 44% of the trabeculectomy group versus 4% of the phacoemulsification group; one third of those undergoing trabeculectomy developed significant cataract within 2 years.
Intraoperative IOP fluctuations and postoperative hypotony are complications the suggested surgical modifications seek to avoid.
monitoring: IOP, postoperative hypotony, cataract development and need for glaucoma medication.

therapies_index.name: phacotrabeculectomy
approved_indications: May be considered for severe PACG.
Studied in PACG with coexisting cataract, including medically uncontrolled disease; the relative benefits of combined versus sequential surgery in severe or advanced disease remain unclear.
therapies_index.administration: The cited comparisons used mitomycin-C.
key_toxicities: Cited comparisons in PACG with cataract reported more complications than with phacoemulsification alone.
monitoring: IOP and postoperative need for glaucoma medication.

therapies_index.name: mitomycin-C
approved_indications: Used with trabeculectomy or phacotrabeculectomy in the PACG surgical approaches discussed.

therapies_index.name: glaucoma drainage device (GDD) surgery
approved_indications: Can be considered when the anterior chamber is sufficiently deep.
therapies_index.administration: In pseudophakic eyes with a shallow chamber, a tube may be placed in the ciliary sulcus.

therapies_index.name: minimally invasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS)
therapies_index.mechanism: Most devices discussed aim to bypass the trabecular meshwork.
therapies_index.administration: Devices are often implanted during cataract extraction, but their effectiveness in angle-closure disease is insufficiently established and they are not licensed for this use in the UK.

therapies_index.name: non-penetrating glaucoma surgery
therapies_index.administration: The guideline reports no useful evidence for its use in angle-closure.

therapies_index.name: laser peripheral iridoplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Can break iridotrabecular contact during an acute angle-closure attack.
approved_indications: May be considered when initial medical treatment does not break an acute attack or corneal oedema prevents iridotomy.
Provides no demonstrated additional IOP-lowering benefit alongside iridotomy in PAC/PACG; it does not replace iridotomy as the principal intervention.
therapies_index.administration: Consider if response is absent or insufficient by 2 hours; acute treatment is also described using an argon/green laser.

therapies_index.name: laser trabeculoplasty
therapies_index.administration: Not currently recommended for PAC or PACG because of poor long-term success.

therapies_index.name: SLT
therapies_index.administration: After PI, it offers no clear additional benefit for IOP control.

therapies_index.name: diode laser cycloablation
approved_indications: Should be considered for acute angle-closure refractory to medical therapy and laser iridoplasty.
therapies_index.administration: Consider when response is absent or insufficient by 2 hours or iridotomy is technically impossible; the guideline recommends that NHS eye departments providing urgent care have a diode laser.

therapies_index.name: trans-scleral cyclophotocoagulation (TSCPC)
approved_indications: Usually reserved for refractory glaucoma; case series suggest it can control IOP during acute attacks unresponsive to standard treatment.

therapies_index.name: micropulse TSCPC
therapies_index.mechanism: Short energy bursts delivered to the ciliary body generate heat for coagulation.
therapies_index.administration: Evidence of effectiveness for PACG is lacking.

therapies_index.name: endoscopic cyclophotocoagulation
therapies_index.administration: The guideline reports no supporting evidence for PACG.

therapies_index.name: diode laser cyclophotocoagulation
approved_indications: Described as an effective alternative treatment for aqueous misdirection in many cases.

therapies_index.name: limbal paracentesis
therapies_index.administration: The guideline states that it has no proven role in acute angle-closure management and may cause harm.
key_toxicities: Severe complications have been reported anecdotally.

therapies_index.name: pars plana vitrectomy
approved_indications: May be required for aqueous misdirection in phakic eyes, with or without lens extraction.
May be considered alongside phacoemulsification in very small eyes with very shallow anterior chambers after discussion with a vitreo-retinal surgeon.

therapies_index.name: Nd:YAG laser vitreolysis/capsulotomy
approved_indications: May be tried for aqueous misdirection in pseudophakic eyes.

therapies_index.name: zonulo-hyaloido-vitrectomy
approved_indications: Described as an effective option for aqueous misdirection.
therapies_index.administration: Can be performed through a peripheral iridectomy or iridotomy via the anterior chamber; a pars plana approach is also possible.

therapies_index.name: G. Dorzolamide 2%/G. Timolol 0.5% combination
approved_indications: Included in the immediate medication regimen for acute angle-closure attributed to pupil block or plateau iris.
therapies_index.administration: Give as stat eye drops: G. Dorzolamide 2%/G. Timolol 0.5% combination.

therapies_index.name: Dorzolamide
approved_indications: Named as a component of the stat combination eye drops in the acute angle-closure pathway.
therapies_index.administration: G. Dorzolamide 2% in combination with G. Timolol 0.5%.

therapies_index.name: Timolol
approved_indications: Named as a component of the stat combination eye drops in the acute angle-closure pathway.
Discussed as an IOP-lowering comparator with prostaglandin analogues in PACG.
therapies_index.administration: G. Timolol 0.5% in combination with G. Dorzolamide 2% in the acute pathway.

therapies_index.name: Apraclonidine
approved_indications: Included among stat eye drops in the acute angle-closure pathway.
therapies_index.administration: G. Apraclonidine 0.5% as stat medication.
monitoring: Before use, ask about angina due to coronary artery disease, previous myocardial infarction and prior coronary artery stenting; the guideline treats these as contraindications.

therapies_index.name: brimonidine
monitoring: Before use, ask about angina due to coronary artery disease, previous myocardial infarction and prior coronary artery stenting; the guideline treats these as contraindications.

therapies_index.name: Pilocarpine
approved_indications: Included in initial medical treatment for acute primary angle-closure attributed to pupil block or plateau iris.
May be beneficial in PACG associated with non-pupil-block or plateau iris mechanisms.
therapies_index.administration: G. Pilocarpine 2% initially, deferred if IOP> 40 mmHg; after the first instillation, an appropriate frequency is every six hours. Intensive drops are not advised. Do not use for lenticular or retro-lenticular angle-closure or to re-constrict the pupil after dilation.
key_toxicities: Can aggravate lenticular or retro-lenticular angle-closure, prolonging pain and delaying IOP control.
After dilation, it may hold the pupil in a mid-dilated position and increase angle-closure risk.
monitoring: Check the mechanism of angle-closure and IOP before administration.

therapies_index.name: acetazolamide
approved_indications: Systemic treatment for early IOP control in acute primary angle-closure.
May be prescribed after pupil dilation in established or probable angle-closure when not contraindicated.
therapies_index.administration: IV Acetazolamide 250mg if IOP> 40mmHg in the acute pathway. After dilation, PO acetazolamide 250mg on leaving the department and another dose at bedtime that night, unless contraindicated.
key_toxicities: Potentially serious drug allergies or side-effects are noted.
monitoring: Establish whether the patient has a history of allergy to sulphonamide medications or severe nephropathy before initial acute treatment.

therapies_index.name: atropine
therapies_index.mechanism: Produces cycloplegia for lenticular or retro-lenticular angle-closure and aqueous misdirection.
approved_indications: Substituted for pilocarpine when lenticular or retro-lenticular causes produce acute angle-closure.
Used as initial medical treatment for aqueous misdirection.
therapies_index.administration: Atropine 1% replaces pilocarpine in the acute care pathway for lenticular or retro-lenticular causes; atropine +/- phenylephrine is described for acute secondary lenticular or retro-lenticular presentations.

therapies_index.name: cyclopentolate
approved_indications: Initial medical treatment for lenticular or retro-lenticular angle-closure.
Initial medical treatment for aqueous misdirection.

therapies_index.name: phenylephrine
approved_indications: May be used with atropine to dilate the pupil in acute secondary lenticular or retro-lenticular angle-closure.
therapies_index.administration: Described as an optional addition to atropine; its use with pilocarpine in provocative testing is discussed but such tests are not recommended.

therapies_index.name: G. Dexamethasone 0.1%
approved_indications: Topical anti-inflammatory treatment after completion of PI in the acute angle-closure pathway.
therapies_index.administration: At minimum, hourly while awake for 24 hours, then 4 x day for one week.

therapies_index.name: G. Prednisolone 1%
approved_indications: Alternative topical anti-inflammatory treatment after completion of PI in the acute angle-closure pathway.
therapies_index.administration: At minimum, hourly while awake for 24 hours, then 4 x day for one week.

therapies_index.name: tropicamide
approved_indications: Used alone for pupil dilation in most patients with established or probable angle-closure.
therapies_index.administration: Use alone for dilation; the guideline describes PO acetazolamide 250mg on departure and another dose at bedtime that night unless contraindicated.

therapies_index.name: mannitol
approved_indications: A hyperosmotic option following initial medical treatment for aqueous misdirection if there are no contraindications.

therapies_index.name: prostaglandin analogues
approved_indications: Medical IOP-lowering treatment for PACG; monotherapy is effective and outperforms timolol.

therapies_index.name: beta blockers
approved_indications: Included among medical treatments for PACG.

therapies_index.name: alpha-agonists
approved_indications: Included among medical treatments for PACG.

therapies_index.name: carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
approved_indications: Included among medical treatments for PACG.

therapies_index.name: analgesia
approved_indications: Immediate symptomatic care for painful acute angle-closure.
therapies_index.administration: Give if required; oral analgesia is also specified in the acute treatment recommendations.

therapies_index.name: anti-emesis
approved_indications: Immediate symptomatic care for nausea or vomiting during acute angle-closure.
therapies_index.administration: Give if required.

therapies_index.name: topiramate
therapies_index.administration: If implicated in atypical angle-closure, discuss a possible change to an alternative medication with the prescribing physician.
key_toxicities: May cause an atypical angle-closure mechanism involving supraciliary effusions and anterior rotation of the ciliary body.
monitoring: Ask directly about its use in suspected atypical angle-closure.

therapies_index.name: antidepressant medication (SSRI and tricyclics)
therapies_index.administration: Advise patients about the increased angle-closure risk and to discuss the need for treatment with the prescribing physician.
key_toxicities: Use is associated with increased risk of angle-closure disease.

therapies_index.name: trimethoprim
monitoring: A history of allergy to this example of a sulphonamide medication should be sought before systemic acetazolamide is used for acute IOP control.

conditions.name: primary angle-closure disease
conditions.description: Primary irido-trabecular contact (ITC) occurs without another ocular or systemic disease causing angle closure. Obstruction of aqueous circulation may occur at the pupil, ciliary body, lens or behind the lens; the latter two locations are generally regarded as secondary mechanisms.
conditions.epidemiology: Angle-closure is uncommon in adults under 40 and very rare in children. It occurs at approximately a 3:1 female-to-male ratio. Asian populations have a greater burden, whereas angle-closure glaucoma is uncommon among Africans.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The spectrum extends from irido-trabecular contact without pressure elevation or visual damage to glaucomatous optic neuropathy. Acute symptomatic crises are a distinct presentation.

subtypes.name: primary angle closure suspect
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Irido-trabecular contact without elevated IOP or glaucomatous optic neuropathy.

subtypes.name: primary angle closure
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Elevated IOP without glaucomatous optic neuropathy.

subtypes.name: primary angle closure glaucoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Glaucomatous optic nerve damage and reproducible visual field loss in an eye with an occluded drainage angle.

subtypes.name: acute angle closure (AAC) crisis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Sudden, symptomatic angle closure requiring urgent assessment and management.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish and monitor drainage-angle anatomy, including assessment for PAS.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Diagnosis and monitoring of angle-closure disease.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: It remains the definitive examination; dynamic gonioscopy provides anatomical information unavailable from the other examinations discussed.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide a rapid, non-contact assessment of limbal anterior chamber depth.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment alongside gonioscopy and case detection in community or primary care.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A limbal chamber depth grade < ¼ meets the angle component of the PACS PLUS referral criteria.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Document angle anatomy and identify ITC, including changes around treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Supplementary assessment, referral triage or follow-up when available.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An image showing ITC meets the angle component of PACS PLUS. AS OCT does not replace gonioscopy for detecting PAS; its ability to predict future glaucoma has not been established.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess anterior-segment anatomy.
Investigate a proposed means of identifying people at increased risk.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Evidence does not support their use for diagnosis or monitoring in PAC/PACG.

pathology_markers.expected_result: Contact between the iris and trabecular meshwork.
pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Defines primary angle closure when another causative ocular or systemic disease is absent.

pathology_markers.expected_result: Acquired adhesions between the iris and drainage-angle structures may develop.
pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Its relevance to subsequent visual loss remains uncertain.

genetic_molecular.clinical_significance: Identified as a gene associated with increased risk of angle-closure disease.
Mutations have been linked to familial angle-closure in white UK citizens.

staging.system: Natural History Staging of Angle-closure Disease

definitions.description: Irido-trabecular contact with normal IOP and no glaucomatous optic neuropathy.
Elevated IOP without glaucomatous optic neuropathy; other ocular disorders may coexist.
A symptomatic acute presentation whose effects on current vision and need for urgent care distinguish it from routine presentations; glaucomatous neuropathy, if present, may have preceded the crisis.
An occluded drainage angle accompanied by pre-laminar optic nerve head abnormalities and reproducible visual field loss.

staging.additional_rules: Assessment of the likely obstruction mechanism complements natural-history staging. The distinction between anterior obstruction at the pupil or ciliary body and posterior obstruction at or behind the lens is particularly important for management.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: After PI, residual ITC alone does not establish a need for another intervention. Follow-up decisions take account of IOP, glaucoma and vision in both eyes.

conditions.name: primary angle closure suspect
conditions.description: The iris contacts the trabecular meshwork while IOP, optic nerve structure and visual function remain normal; acquired PAS are absent in the description of this initial stage.
conditions.epidemiology: In the ZAP study, untreated eyes had 36/889 new cases over 6 years, reported as 8 new cases/1,000 years. New PAS accounted for 30/889 eyes, elevated IOP for 5/889 eyes and acute crises for 5/889 eyes; three eyes reached both the IOP and PAS endpoints. No incident glaucomatous optic neuropathy occurred during the six-year follow-up. Applicability of these findings to nonChinese populations remains unproven.
conditions.clinical_presentation: An occludable angle may be found despite normal IOP, optic disc appearance and visual field status.

subtypes.name: PACS PLUS
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An angle meeting the specified LACD or AS OCT criterion together with at least one listed additional risk factor.

subtypes.name: PACS MINUS
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The specified angle finding without a PLUS factor and without meeting NICE glaucoma referral guidance.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm angle closure and assess for PAS.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The definitive examination for angle-closure disease.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess limbal chamber depth for case detection.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A grade < ¼ satisfies one possible PACS PLUS angle criterion.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify and document ITC.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When available as a supplementary or triage examination.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Demonstrated ITC satisfies the alternative PACS PLUS angle criterion; this examination does not replace gonioscopy for PAS.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine whether pressure is elevated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Normal IOP is part of the suspect-stage definition.

diagnostic_workup.test: Optic disc and visual field assessment
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Check for glaucomatous damage.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Normal findings are expected in PACS.

pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Incident PAS was the most frequent progression endpoint in the cited trial, although its immediate implications for vision appeared limited.

staging.system: Natural History Staging of Angle-closure Disease

definitions.description: Irido-trabecular contact with normal IOP and no glaucomatous optic neuropathy.

prognostic_tools.name: PACS PLUS
components: Limbal chamber depth grade < ¼ or AS OCT showing ITC
Only one good eye whose visual deterioration could threaten independent living or livelihood
Vulnerable adult who may not report symptoms
Family history of significant angle closure disease
Diabetes or another condition requiring regular pupil dilation
Antidepressants or medication with an anticholinergic action
Residence or work where prompt emergency ophthalmic care is unavailable

risk_groups.criteria: The specified angle finding and one of the additional factors.
The specified angle finding, no PLUS factor and no indication for referral under NICE glaucoma guidance.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: PACS PLUS prompts referral to the Hospital Eye Service; people meeting PACS MINUS criteria are advised to obtain an annual NHS sight test.

follow_up.schedule: An annual NHS sight test is advised for PACS MINUS.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: After PI, residual ITC may inform follow-up risk assessment, but ITC alone does not support further intervention.

conditions.name: primary angle closure
conditions.description: This stage has elevated IOP, currently or previously, and/or developed PAS, without glaucomatous optic nerve damage or visual field abnormality.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Lens opacity or retinal vascular disease may coexist despite the absence of glaucomatous neuropathy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Diagnose and monitor angle closure, including PAS.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Definitive angle examination.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify elevated pressure and guide management.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The EAGLE trial included PAC with IOP above 30 mmHg; the surgical recommendation specifies IOP > 30mmHg.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Supplement angle assessment and document ITC.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Cannot replace gonioscopy for detecting PAS.

diagnostic_workup.test: Optic nerve and visual field assessment
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine whether glaucomatous damage has developed.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Glaucomatous neuropathy is absent at the PAC stage.

pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Can indicate established angle-closure disease, although its visual prognostic significance is uncertain.

staging.system: Natural History Staging of Angle-closure Disease

definitions.description: Elevated IOP without glaucomatous optic neuropathy.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: Following PI, additional intervention for residual ITC is not recommended unless IOP rises, GON worsens or symptomatic attacks recur.

conditions.name: primary angle closure glaucoma
conditions.description: An occluded drainage angle accompanies structural injury at the pre-laminar optic nerve head and reproducible visual field loss. Previously detected elevated IOP or PAS is not required in every patient.
conditions.epidemiology: A systematic review estimated prevalence at 0.4% among white European adults aged over 40, corresponding to 130,000 people in the UK and 1.6 million across Europe; demographic projections suggested an increase of 20% per decade. The guide estimates approximately one case in 6 of glaucoma in the UK may be PACG. A global projection attributed bilateral severe visual impairment in 2020 to PACG in 5.3 million people. PACG produces severe visual loss more often than POAG.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Glaucomatous optic nerve changes and reproducible visual field defects occur with angle occlusion. Marked pain or other acute symptoms are not necessary for disease to be present.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish angle anatomy and detect PAS.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Remains the definitive examination.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess anterior chamber depth as an additional examination.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Alongside gonioscopy or during case detection.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A shallower anterior chamber is a risk factor for PACG.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Supplement assessment and document angle anatomy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Cannot substitute for gonioscopy to detect PAS.

diagnostic_workup.test: Optic nerve head examination and visual field assessment
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish structural and functional glaucomatous damage.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Pre-laminar structural abnormalities together with reproducible visual field loss define glaucoma in this setting.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess pressure and disease control.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: PACG can occur without previously detected elevated IOP.

pathology_markers.expected_result: Glaucomatous structural optic nerve abnormalities with reproducible visual field loss.
pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Distinguishes PACG from earlier angle-closure stages.

genetic_molecular.clinical_significance: The guide identifies this gene as associated with increased angle-closure disease risk, not as a diagnostic test for PACG.
Mutations have been linked to familial angle-closure in white UK citizens; the guide does not establish their ability to predict glaucomatous visual loss.

staging.system: Natural History Staging of Angle-closure Disease

definitions.description: The final stage, characterised by glaucomatous optic neuropathy with an occluded drainage angle.

staging.additional_rules: Alternative explanations for impaired vision should be considered and investigated when necessary.

conditions.name: acute angle closure (AAC) crisis
conditions.description: Sudden obstruction of the drainage angle causes pronounced ocular hypertension and constitutes an ophthalmic emergency. An acute presentation may occur with or without pre-existing glaucomatous neuropathy.
conditions.epidemiology: Reported annual crisis incidence is between 2 – 5 /100,000/year in European populations, 12 – 16/100,000/year in Chinese populations and 6 – 7 /100,000/year among South and Southeast Asian people; the cited incidence studies generally concern people aged 30 years and older and often rely on hospital episodes. Following an acute presentation, a cited report found that 9% later became blind from glaucoma, with a similar proportion experiencing visual loss from unoperated cataract.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Patients may develop substantial ocular pain, sudden reduction or loss of vision, nausea and/or vomiting. Blurred vision and haloes may occur but are not specific. Lens opacity or an unresponsive dilated pupil after iris ischaemia may affect current vision.

subtypes.name: plateau iris
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Anterior non-pupil-block obstruction involving ciliary processes or peripheral iris crowding.

subtypes.name: lens-induced angle-closure
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A secondary lenticular mechanism that requires differentiation because pilocarpine may aggravate it.

subtypes.name: retro-lenticular angle-closure
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A secondary posterior mechanism that requires differentiation because pilocarpine may aggravate it.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm elevated pressure and assess response to initial treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Immediately when an acute crisis is suspected and during treatment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Confirmation of elevated IOP together with angle closure is a central initial management decision.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm angle closure and look for secondary lenticular or retro-lenticular mechanisms.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Immediately in suspected acute angle closure.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Marked asymmetry of central anterior chamber depth is a key clue to a lenticular or retro-lenticular cause.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify contraindications to treatment and possible drug-induced secondary angle closure.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During initial assessment; ask directly about topiramate in atypical presentations.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: topiramate use may indicate a secondary mechanism involving supraciliary effusions.

staging.system: Natural History Staging of Angle-closure Disease

definitions.description: An acute symptomatic variant requiring expeditious care because current visual function can be affected, sometimes reversibly.

staging.additional_rules: Glaucomatous neuropathy observed during a crisis may have existed before the acute pressure rise.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: The fellow eye is at substantial risk of a subsequent acute episode.

conditions.name: plateau iris
conditions.description: Angle obstruction arises at the ciliary body and/or through peripheral iris crowding. This anterior mechanism may coexist with pupil block.
conditions.epidemiology: When PACG occurs in adults under 40, the guide considers a plateau iris mechanism predominant.
conditions.clinical_presentation: It may contribute to angle closure even when a non-pupil-block mechanism is suspected, including during an acute presentation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess drainage-angle anatomy and angle closure.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Provides dynamic anatomical information.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess anterior-segment anatomy.

staging.additional_rules: Classified among the anterior locations of obstruction in the guide's mechanism framework.

conditions.name: lens-induced angle-closure
conditions.description: A secondary mechanism in which an intumescent, white or unstable lens obstructs aqueous circulation. The guide distinguishes it from primary angle closure in which lens size or position contributes to a shallow chamber.
conditions.epidemiology: Lenticular block accounts for approximately 5% of angleclosure presentations in the UK.
conditions.clinical_presentation: An acute presentation may include elevated pressure and marked asymmetry of central anterior chamber depth. Pilocarpine typically worsens this mechanism.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a possible secondary lenticular mechanism.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Pronounced asymmetry is an important clinical clue.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm and monitor pressure elevation.
Identify the causative lens abnormality.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When lenticular angle closure is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A white, intumescent or unstable lens supports the secondary lens-induced mechanism described in the guide.

staging.additional_rules: Obstruction at the lens is classified as a posterior rather than an anterior level in the mechanism framework.

conditions.name: retro-lenticular angle-closure
conditions.description: A secondary mechanism arising behind the lens, within the vitreous or retina. The guide identifies massive vitreous or sub-retinal haemorrhage, inflammatory effusions and tumours as possible causes.
conditions.epidemiology: Retro-lenticular block accounts for approximately 1% of angleclosure presentations in the UK.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Acute symptoms or high pressure may occur. Marked asymmetry of central anterior chamber depth can suggest this mechanism; pilocarpine typically aggravates it.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Look for a posterior secondary mechanism.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Marked asymmetry supports consideration of a lenticular or retro-lenticular cause.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm and monitor elevated pressure.

staging.additional_rules: Obstruction behind the lens is the most posterior level in the guide's mechanism framework.

conditions.name: Aqueous misdirection/malignant glaucoma
conditions.description: Choroidal expansion and resistance to aqueous movement from the posterior to anterior segment displace the irido-lens diaphragm forward and close the anterior chamber angle.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Sudden shallowing of the anterior chamber, particularly after surgery, should raise suspicion. IOP can be normal. Short axial length, angle-closure disease and a phakic lens are described risk factors.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify sudden shallowing and angle closure.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Especially when abrupt shallowing occurs post-operatively.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The finding prompts consideration of aqueous misdirection.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterise the presentation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A normal result does not exclude the diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine whether a patent peripheral iridotomy is present.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: The guide states that good evidence about prevention and management is lacking.

conditions.name: nanophthalmos
conditions.description: The guide uses this term for eyes with an axial length of less than 20.00 mm.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Very small eyes may have particularly shallow anterior chambers. Underlying amblyopia or foveal hypoplasia can limit visual results after lens or cataract surgery.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure axial length and inform IOL selection.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment of small eyes, particularly before lens or cataract surgery.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An axial length of less than 20.00 mm meets the guide's definition of nanophthalmos. Biometry in very small eyes is less accurate.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a very shallow chamber relevant to surgical planning.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before lens or cataract surgery in very small eyes.

long_term_effects: Amblyopia or foveal hypoplasia may limit visual acuity after surgery.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The guide reports that lens or cataract surgery complications may occur in 30% of cases or more, including aqueous misdirection, zonular dialysis, cystoid macular oedema and choroidal effusions.

conditions.name: drug induced
conditions.description: An atypical, secondary angle-closure mechanism may arise from medication. The guide specifically describes topiramate-associated supraciliary effusions and forward rotation of the ciliary body.
conditions.clinical_presentation: topiramate is identified as a cause to consider in an atypical presentation; the guide notes that bilateral angle closure from a posterior-segment mechanism has been regularly reported in association with its use. Antidepressant medication, including SSRI and tricyclics, is associated with increased angle-closure risk, without being assigned the same mechanism.

subtypes.name: topiramate-associated angle-closure
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Supraciliary effusions with anterior rotation of the ciliary body may cause an atypical presentation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a possible drug-associated cause.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Direct questioning should establish whether the patient uses topiramate.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm the acute presentation and assess its mechanism.

artifacts.clinical_relevance: Helps readers locate the sections on diagnosis, treatment, follow-up and risks.
