artifacts.summary: Pairs diagnostic codes with angle-closure conditions and related drug effects.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Distinguishes codes for suspected, established, acute and other forms of angle-closure disease.

artifacts.title: Natural History Staging of Angle-closure Disease
artifacts.description: Stage a: Primary angle closure suspect has iridotrabecular contact, normal intraocular pressure and no glaucomatous optic neuropathy. Stage b: Primary angle closure has elevated intraocular pressure without glaucomatous optic neuropathy; other ocular disease may coexist. Stage c: Acute angle closure (AAC) crisis requires urgent management because of its acute symptoms and potentially reversible effect on current vision; glaucomatous optic neuropathy may also be present. Stage d: Primary angle closure glaucoma has an occluded drainage angle, structural abnormalities of the pre-laminar optic nerve head and reproducible visual field loss.
artifacts.summary: Defines the clinical stages used to describe the natural history of primary angle-closure disease.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Supports classification according to pressure, optic nerve damage, visual function and the need for urgent care.

artifacts.title: Underlying mechanism of angle closure
artifacts.description: Identify the level obstructing aqueous circulation: a. pupil block; b. ciliary body involvement, including plateau iris or peripheral iris crowding; c. lens-level obstruction or lens intumescence; or d. obstruction behind the lens, within the vitreous or retina. For management, distinguish anterior mechanisms, a and b, from posterior mechanisms, c and d.
artifacts.summary: Organizes angle-closure mechanisms by the anatomical site of aqueous-flow obstruction.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: The distinction matters because lenticular and retro-lenticular presentations are typically aggravated by pilocarpine, whereas the guideline identifies cycloplegia as their initial medical treatment.

artifacts.title: “PACS PLUS” Criteria for Referral of People with Suspected Occluded Angles to the Hospital Eye Service
artifacts.description: Step 1: Establish either limbal chamber depth grade < ¼ or irido-trabecular contact (ITC) on anterior segment OCT. Step 2: Check for at least one additional criterion: only one “good eye” whose deterioration could threaten independent living or livelihood; a vulnerable adult who might not report symptoms; family history of significant angle closure disease; high hypermetropia (> + 6.00 dioptres); diabetes or another condition requiring regular pupil dilation; antidepressant or anticholinergic medication use; or residence or work in a remote location without rapid access to emergency ophthalmic care. Step 3: If the angle criterion and an additional criterion are present, refer to the Hospital Eye Service as “PACS PLUS”. If the angle criterion is present without an additional criterion and NICE glaucoma referral guidelines are not met, advise an annual NHS sight test as “PACS MINUS”. Elevated IOP or glaucoma provides a separate basis for referral.
artifacts.summary: Sets out angle findings and additional risk factors used to decide whether a person with suspected occluded angles should be referred.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Separates people who warrant hospital assessment from those advised to continue annual sight testing.

artifacts.title: Acute Angle Closure Care Pathway (pupillary block or plateau iris mechanism)
artifacts.description: Step 1: Provide analgesia and anti-emesis when needed. Confirm that angle closure has raised intraocular pressure, assess for lenticular or retro-lenticular secondary causes, and identify allergies or contraindications. Step 2: Give initial G. Dorzolamide 2%/G. Timolol 0.5% combination, G. Apraclonidine 0.5% and G. Pilocarpine 2%; defer G. Pilocarpine 2% if IOP> 40 mmHg. Give IV Acetazolamide 250mg if IOP> 40mmHg. For lenticular or retro-lenticular causes, substitute Atropine 1% for pilocarpine. Step 3: Reassess after 30-60 minutes. If the cornea is clear and the patient is comfortable enough for laser treatment, perform laser peripheral iridotomy in both eyes. Step 4: After PI, start G. Dexamethasone 0.1% or G. Prednisolone 1% at least hourly while awake for 24 hours, then 4 x day for one week. Step 5: If response is absent or inadequate by 2 hours, or corneal oedema prevents iridotomy, consider laser peripheral iridoplasty or diode laser cycloablation. Direct treatment of secondary cases toward their underlying pathology.
artifacts.summary: Provides the sequence for initial symptom control, assessment, medication, reassessment and laser treatment during an acute angle-closure crisis.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Makes identification of secondary mechanisms and treatment contraindications part of urgent care, while specifying when to escalate if initial treatment is unsuccessful.

recommendations.statement: Consider laser iridotomy even when angle closure appears to involve a mechanism other than pupil block.
recommendations.context: Pupil block and plateau iris mechanisms can coexist.
recommendations.rationale: An apparent non-pupil-block mechanism does not rule out a contribution from pupil block.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1 Terminology & Disease Definitions — Underlying mechanism of angle closure — Practice point

recommendations.statement: Advise first-degree relatives of people with significant primary angle-closure disease, rather than PACS alone, to have regular community optometric examinations. Refer relatives meeting current referral criteria to hospital eye services for consideration of prophylactic laser iridotomy.
recommendations.context: First-degree relatives of patients with significant primary angle-closure disease.
recommendations.rationale: Occluded drainage angles and angle-closure disease show familial clustering.

recommendations.statement: Retain gonioscopy as the definitive examination for diagnosing and monitoring angle-closure disease.
recommendations.rationale: Dynamic examination provides information about drainage-angle anatomy.

recommendations.statement: Use anterior segment OCT (AS OCT) to supplement, rather than replace, gonioscopy; gonioscopy remains necessary to detect PAS.
recommendations.context: Diagnosis and monitoring of angle-closure disease.
recommendations.rationale: AS OCT can document angle anatomy, but it cannot substitute for gonioscopy when assessing PAS.

recommendations.statement: Continue using gonioscopy to diagnose angle-closure disease.
recommendations.context: Summary of diagnostic evidence.

recommendations.statement: Use AS-OCT as an adjunct to gonioscopy, including to document findings and potentially facilitate follow-up around treatment, but not as a replacement for diagnostic gonioscopy.
recommendations.rationale: It provides a record of angle anatomy that can be reviewed during follow-up.

recommendations.statement: In secondary care, AS-OCT may serve as a triage examination during referral refinement to determine whether gonioscopy is needed.
recommendations.context: Secondary-care referral refinement.

recommendations.statement: Do not use provocative tests to diagnose or monitor PAC/PACG.
recommendations.context: The guideline finds no evidence supporting this use.
recommendations.rationale: Provocative tests have not consistently identified people at substantial risk of angle-closure disease.

recommendations.statement: Refer people with suspected occluded angles to the Hospital Eye Service when the angle meets the PACS PLUS angle criterion and at least one PLUS criterion is present.
recommendations.context: The angle criterion is a limbal chamber depth grade < ¼ or anterior segment OCT evidence of irido-trabecular contact (ITC). PLUS criteria are an only good eye whose visual deterioration could threaten independent living or livelihood; a vulnerable adult who might not report ocular or visual symptoms; family history of significant angle-closure disease; high hypermetropia (> + 6.00 dioptres); diabetes or another reason for regular pupil dilation; antidepressant or anticholinergic medication use; or residence or work where emergency ophthalmic care is not rapidly accessible.
recommendations.rationale: These additional factors identify people for hospital referral despite the generally low risk associated with occluded angles alone.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.3 Diagnosis — “PACS PLUS” Criteria for Referral of People with Suspected Occluded Angles to the Hospital Eye Service

recommendations.statement: Advise an individual meeting the specified angle criterion but no PLUS criterion and no NICE glaucoma referral criterion to obtain an annual NHS sight test.
recommendations.context: PACS MINUS.

recommendations.statement: Prefer phacoemulsification lens extraction to laser PI for PAC with IOP > 30mmHg.
recommendations.rationale: In EAGLE, lens extraction provided better disease-control, economic and patient-reported outcomes than laser iridotomy.

recommendations.statement: Do not add goniosynechialysis to phacoemulsification as a routine intervention.
recommendations.rationale: The cited randomised trials found no additional benefit from GSL.

recommendations.statement: Do not stop anti-coagulants solely for PI when INR < 3.
recommendations.context: Patients undergoing PI.
recommendations.rationale: Bleeding rates did not appear to differ when anticoagulants were continued under the stated INR condition.

recommendations.statement: PI may be performed at either a superior (12 o’clock) or temporal location.
recommendations.context: Choice of iridotomy site in relation to dysphotopsia.
recommendations.rationale: Studies have not produced consistent evidence that PI location affects dysphotopsia.

recommendations.statement: Do not undertake an additional intervention for residual ITC alone after PI; residual ITC may instead inform the intensity of follow-up.
recommendations.context: Residual ITC is reported in 20-80% of cases after PI.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence does not support further treatment based solely on this finding.

recommendations.statement: Do not add laser peripheral iridoplasty for the purpose of lowering IOP in PAC/PACG.
recommendations.context: Use in addition to laser iridotomy.
recommendations.rationale: The cited randomised trials showed no additional IOP-control benefit.

recommendations.statement: Do not undertake population-wide screening and prophylactic treatment for precursors of PACG in high-risk Asian populations.
recommendations.rationale: The cited screening trial found no difference in incident glaucoma between screened and control groups.

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely offer prophylactic laser PI to everyone with PACS solely because of their PACS classification.
recommendations.context: In the ZAP trial, laser PI reduced incident PAC disease, but most participants were unlikely to gain much individual benefit.
recommendations.rationale: Incident disease was uncommon even in the high-risk population studied.

recommendations.statement: Advise laser PI for people with PACS PLUS additional risk factors until further evidence becomes available.
recommendations.context: Examples include an only eye, family history of significant angle-closure disease, high hypermetropia, diabetes or another reason for regular pupil dilation, antidepressant or anticholinergic medication use, and residence or work where emergency ophthalmic care cannot be accessed promptly.

recommendations.statement: Do not advise laser PI for most people with PACS who have no additional risk factors.
recommendations.rationale: The risk of incident disease is low for most such individuals.

recommendations.statement: Attempt laser iridotomy without delay in the fellow eye of a patient with an acute angle-closure crisis, once IOP is controlled and before discharge.
recommendations.context: Contralateral eye after an acute crisis.
recommendations.rationale: A subsequent acute crisis can occur in the fellow eye soon after the initial presentation.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.4 Management — Laser iridotomy in the fellow eye of people suffering acute angle-closure — Practice point

recommendations.statement: Perform laser iridotomy in every contralateral eye when its fellow eye has experienced acute symptomatic angle-closure, at the time the acute episode is treated.
recommendations.rationale: The untreated fellow eye has a high risk of a similar attack.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.4 Management — Laser iridotomy in the fellow eye of people suffering acute angle-closure

recommendations.statement: In acute angle-closure, consider a secondary lenticular or retro-lenticular mechanism when central anterior chamber depth is asymmetric; treat these presentations with pupil dilation rather than pilocarpine.
recommendations.context: Acute symptomatic presentation or raised IOP from a suspected secondary mechanism.
recommendations.rationale: Pilocarpine may aggravate lenticular or retro-lenticular angle closure.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.4 Management — Acute angle-closure crisis — Practice point

recommendations.statement: Immediately give systemic acetazolamide, topical pilocarpine and other ocular hypotensive medication together for acute primary angle-closure; also provide topical steroids, oral analgesia and antiemetics as required.
recommendations.context: First-line treatment of acute primary angle-closure.

recommendations.statement: Consider argon/green laser iridoplasty if medical treatment does not terminate the acute attack.
recommendations.context: Second-line treatment.
recommendations.rationale: In the cited trial, iridoplasty reduced IOP more quickly initially, although the groups did not differ by two hours.

recommendations.statement: Consider cyclodiode laser for acute cases unresponsive to both medical therapy and ALPI.
recommendations.context: Refractory acute attack.

recommendations.statement: Attempt laser iridotomy or surgical iridectomy in both eyes after the initial acute attack resolves.
Do not rely on paracentesis to manage acute angle-closure.
recommendations.rationale: Its role has not been established, and it may cause harm.

recommendations.statement: Offer early phacoemulsification to patients with cataract after acute angle-closure once IOP is controlled and the cornea has cleared, approximately 1 to 4 weeks after presentation.
recommendations.context: Acute angle-closure with cataract.

recommendations.statement: Use clear lens phaco rather than PI as the primary intervention for PACG.
recommendations.rationale: The guideline reports superior outcomes with clear lens phaco compared with PI.

recommendations.statement: Do not expect adding goniosynechialysis (GSL) to phacoemulsification to reduce the need for antiglaucoma eyedrops compared with phacoemulsification alone.
recommendations.rationale: The cited evidence did not show a reduction in eyedrop use from the combined procedure.

recommendations.statement: Prefer phacoemulsification clear lens extraction or cataract surgery to trabeculectomy or phaco-trab in PACG on safety grounds; trabeculectomy or phacotrabeculectomy may nevertheless be considered for severe disease.
recommendations.rationale: The cited comparisons associated trabeculectomy-containing approaches with more complications.

recommendations.statement: Consider that early phaco may provide greater benefit than PI for patients with AAC and PACG who also have cataract.
Perform laser PI promptly for AAC and the fellow eye.
Do not expect a clear additional benefit from laser peripheral iridoplasty alongside PI in PACG.
Do not expect a clear IOP-control benefit from SLT after PI.
Do not select PI location or size on the expectation that either will change the frequency of dysphotopsia.
recommendations.rationale: Neither characteristic appears to affect dysphotopsia rates.

recommendations.statement: Prefer sequential argon/YAG PI for dark irides, including those of patients of Asian/African descent.
Use prostaglandin monotherapy as an effective IOP-lowering treatment in PACG; it performs better than timolol.
recommendations.rationale: The cited studies found greater IOP reduction with prostaglandin analogues than with timolol monotherapy after LPI.

recommendations.statement: No PGA offers a benefit over another.
recommendations.rationale: The guideline reports no benefit of one PGA over another.

recommendations.statement: Remain aware of racial variation in biometric and iris anatomy without assuming that different racial groups require different management.
recommendations.context: The guideline finds no evidence supporting race-specific differences in management.
recommendations.rationale: No race-specific management pathway has been established through objective research.

recommendations.statement: Do not undertake further treatment solely because residual ITC persists after PI; the finding may be used to stratify follow-up for PAC disease.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence does not support intervention based on residual ITC alone.

recommendations.statement: Do not recommend an additional intervention for residual ITC unless IOP has demonstrably risen, GON has worsened or symptomatic attacks have recurred.
recommendations.context: Follow-up after PI.

recommendations.statement: Offer phacoemulsification and IOL in accordance with cataract surgery guidance.
recommendations.context: Cataract in a patient with angle-closure disease.

recommendations.statement: Explain the additional surgical risk to patients with an axial length of < 21.00.
recommendations.context: Lens or cataract surgery in short eyes.
recommendations.rationale: The guideline reports increasing complication rates with shorter axial length below 21mm.

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely perform laser peripheral iridotomy before phacoemulsification and IOL.
recommendations.rationale: The guideline finds no evidence supporting preoperative iridotomy.

recommendations.statement: Counsel patients with nanophthalmos that complications of lens or cataract surgery may occur in 30% of cases or more, including aqueous misdirection, zonular dialysis, cystoid macular oedema and choroidal effusions.
recommendations.context: Preoperative counselling.

recommendations.statement: Clearly explain the risk of an unexpected refractive result when counselling patients with nanophthalmos.
recommendations.context: Biometry in small eyes is difficult to perform accurately.

recommendations.statement: Consider performing a surgical iridectomy during lens or cataract extraction in eyes with nanophthalmos.
recommendations.rationale: The procedure may reduce postoperative pupil block and aid management if aqueous misdirection develops.

recommendations.statement: Account for the possibility that a substantial proportion of patients with nanophthalmos undergoing lens or cataract surgery will not attain BCVA > 6/12.
recommendations.context: Visual-prognosis counselling.
recommendations.rationale: Underlying amblyopia or foveal hypoplasia may limit postoperative vision.

recommendations.statement: Following discussion with a vitreo-retinal surgeon, consider pars plana vitrectomy at the same time as phacoemulsification for very small eyes with very shallow anterior chambers.
Initially dilate the pupil with atropine +/- phenylephrine when secondary lenticular or retro-lenticular angle-closure presents with acute symptoms or high pressure.
recommendations.context: Secondary lenticular or retro-lenticular obstruction.
recommendations.rationale: Pilocarpine may worsen these posterior mechanisms of obstruction.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.13 Differences in management of four levels of “block” — Practice point

special_populations.considerations: The guideline defines nanophthalmos as an axial length of less than 20.00 mm. Lens or cataract surgery may cause complications in 30% of cases or more, including aqueous misdirection, zonular dialysis, cystoid macular oedema and choroidal effusions. Biometry is difficult, refractive outcomes are less predictable, and underlying amblyopia or foveal hypoplasia may prevent BCVA > 6/12 in a significant proportion of patients.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Explain the surgical and refractive risks. Consider surgical iridectomy during lens or cataract extraction to reduce postoperative pupil block and facilitate treatment of aqueous misdirection. For very small eyes with very shallow anterior chambers, consider pars plana vitrectomy at the same time as phacoemulsification after discussion with a vitreo-retinal surgeon.

special_populations.population: Patients with shorter axial length undergoing cataract surgery
special_populations.considerations: Below 21mm axial length, the complication rate doubles with every 1 mm reduction in axial length. Biometry in very small eyes is less accurate, which affects intraocular lens selection and discussion of the likely refractive outcome.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Discuss and document the additional surgical risk, and account for reduced biometric accuracy when selecting an intraocular lens.

special_populations.population: Patients with diabetes requiring repeated pupil dilation
special_populations.considerations: Repeated diabetic retinopathy screening examinations may increase the cumulative risk of acute angle-closure. Diabetic retinopathy screening accounts for more UK cases of acute angle-closure than any other identifiable health event cited in the guideline.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Consider identifying patients at risk and arranging glaucoma specialist review to assess whether prophylactic laser iridotomy is appropriate.

special_populations.population: Patients with established or probable angle-closure requiring pupil dilation
special_populations.considerations: Dilation can be performed safely in most cases. Pilocarpine used to constrict the pupil afterward may hold it in a mid-dilated position and increase angle-closure risk.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Use tropicamide alone for dilation in most cases. On departure, prescribe PO acetazolamide 250mg and a further dose at bedtime that night unless contraindicated. Do not use pilocarpine to re-constrict the pupil after dilation.

special_populations.population: First degree relatives of patients with significant primary angle-closure disease
special_populations.considerations: Occluded drainage angles and angle-closure disease are heritable. The guideline distinguishes relatives of patients with significant disease from relatives of primary angle-closure suspects; whether family history itself increases the risk of glaucomatous vision loss remains unknown.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Advise regular community optometric reviews. Refer to hospital eye services for consideration of prophylactic laser iridotomy if current referral criteria are met.

special_populations.considerations: Additional risk circumstances include having only one “good eye” whose deterioration could threaten independence or livelihood; being a vulnerable adult who may not report symptoms; a family history of significant angle closure disease; high hypermetropia (> + 6.00 dioptres); diabetes or another condition requiring regular pupil dilation; use of antidepressants or medication with an anticholinergic action; or living or working remotely without rapid access to emergency ophthalmic care.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Refer those meeting the specified angle criteria and at least one additional criterion to the Hospital Eye Service. Laser PI is advised for PACS PLUS additional risk factor(s).

special_populations.population: People with PACS and no additional risk factors
special_populations.considerations: For most people in this group, the risk of sight-threatening progression is low.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Laser PI is not advised for most. If the specified angle characteristics are present but no PACS PLUS criterion or NICE glaucoma referral criterion is met, advise an annual NHS sight test.

special_populations.population: Fellow eyes of patients with acute angle-closure
special_populations.considerations: The contralateral eye has a high risk of a similar acute episode. Laser iridotomy appears to prevent long-term IOP rises in around 90% of these eyes.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Attempt laser iridotomy in the fellow eye without delay, when the acute episode is treated and before discharge once IOP is controlled.

special_populations.population: Patients with dark irides, including those of Asian or African descent
special_populations.considerations: The guideline notes racial variation in iris anatomy but states that race-specific management pathways have not been established or demonstrated by objective research.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Sequential argon/YAG PI is preferred for dark irides.

special_populations.population: Patients over 50 years of age with mild to moderate PACG or PAC with IOP > 30 mmHg
special_populations.considerations: Clear lens extraction can be considered as initial management. The guideline notes uncertainty about applying the EAGLE findings to non-Chinese/non-European populations.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Consider clear lens extraction as the initial intervention in this population. Decisions to extract the lens for angle-closure control should involve a consultant with a specialist interest in glaucoma.

special_populations.population: Patients with medically uncontrolled PACG without cataract, particularly younger patients with accommodative ability
special_populations.considerations: Preserving accommodative ability is relevant when selecting surgery. In the cited small trial, trabeculectomy required on average 1.1 fewer drugs after surgery than phacoemulsification, but surgical complications were higher with trabeculectomy (44% vs. 4% respectively).
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Trabeculectomy with mitomycin C may be indicated.

special_populations.population: Patients with cataract and acute angle-closure
special_populations.considerations: A cited trial in patients with cataract and visual acuity of ≤6/15 who achieved IOP ≤30 mmHg within 24 hours found that phaco/IOL may provide better IOP stability than LPI.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer early phacoemulsification once IOP is controlled and the cornea is clear, approximately 1 to 4 weeks after presentation.

special_populations.population: Patients with lenticular or retro-lenticular angle-closure
special_populations.considerations: These secondary mechanisms may present with marked asymmetry of central anterior chamber depth. Pilocarpine typically worsens the obstruction.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For an acute presentation or high pressure, initially dilate the pupil with atropine +/- phenylephrine rather than pilocarpine. The acute care pathway specifies substituting Atropine 1% for pilocarpine when lenticular or retro-lenticular causes are present.

special_populations.population: Patients with aqueous misdirection after surgery
special_populations.considerations: Suspect this condition when the anterior chamber suddenly becomes shallow, particularly postoperatively; IOP can be normal. Short axial length, angle-closure and a phakic lens status are risk factors.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Start cycloplegics with atropine or cyclopentolate and systemic and/or topical aqueous-production suppressants, followed by a hyperosmotic agent such as mannitol if not contraindicated. Ensure a patent peripheral iridotomy. Phakic eyes may need pars plana vitrectomy with or without lens extraction; Nd:YAG laser vitreolysis/capsulotomy may be tried in pseudophakic eyes.

special_populations.population: Patients with coronary artery disease causing angina, prior myocardial infarction or prior coronary artery stenting
special_populations.considerations: The guideline treats each of these histories as a contraindication to apraclonidine or brimonidine.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Ask about these histories before choosing treatment; do not use apraclonidine or brimonidine when they are present.

special_populations.population: Patients with suspected sulphonamide medication allergy or severe nephropathy
special_populations.considerations: Potentially serious allergies and adverse effects matter when considering systemic acetazolamide.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Establish whether there is a history of allergy to sulphonamide medications such as trimethoprim or severe nephropathy before using systemic acetazolamide.

special_populations.population: Patients using antidepressants or medication with an anticholinergic action
special_populations.considerations: Antidepressant medication, including SSRI and tricyclics, is associated with increased angle-closure risk. Such medication use is also a PACS PLUS referral criterion.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Advise patients of the excess risk and ask them to discuss the need for antidepressant medication with the prescribing physician.

special_populations.population: Patients using topiramate who present with atypical angle-closure
special_populations.considerations: An idiosyncratic reaction to topiramate may produce supraciliary effusions and ciliary body rotation. The guideline identifies this as a regularly reported cause of bilateral angle-closure involving posterior mechanisms.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Ask directly about topiramate use in suspected atypical cases and discuss the possibility of an alternative medication with the prescribing physician. Direct care at the underlying drug-induced process.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People with suspected occluded angles who meet the angle criteria for “PACS PLUS” and have at least one additional listed risk factor.
decision_rules: The angle criterion is either a limbal chamber depth grade < ¼ or anterior segment OCT showing irido-trabecular contact (ITC).

Refer to the Hospital Eye Service when an angle criterion is accompanied by an “only eye” whose visual deterioration could threaten independence or livelihood; vulnerability that may prevent reporting symptoms; a family history of significant angle closure disease; high hypermetropia (> + 6.00 dioptres); diabetes or another need for regular pupil dilation; use of antidepressants or medication with an anticholinergic action; or residence or work where emergency ophthalmic care is not rapidly accessible.
Until additional evidence is available, offer preventive laser PI to people with PACS PLUS risk factors.

recommended_regimens.name: laser PI
recommended_regimens.summary: Preventive treatment is advised for PACS with additional risk factors.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Vulnerable adults who might not report ocular or visual symptoms are included among the referral groups.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People meeting the specified angle criteria but having no “PACS PLUS” risk factor and not meeting NICE glaucoma referral criteria.
decision_rules: Advise an annual NHS sight test rather than referral solely because of the angle finding.
Refer according to NICE guidance if raised IOP or glaucoma provides a separate indication.

not_recommended.name: laser PI
not_recommended.reason: Routine prophylaxis is not advised for most people with PACS without additional risk factors. The ZAP study found that treatment reduced incident PAC disease, but events were uncommon and most people were likely to gain little benefit.

not_recommended.name: Population-wide screening and prophylaxis
not_recommended.reason: The cited Mongolia trial found no difference in incident glaucoma between its screened intervention group and untreated control group.

response_assessment.interpretation: Applies to people described as “PACS MINUS” who do not otherwise meet NICE glaucoma referral criteria.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In ZAP, laser iridotomy reduced incident angle-closure disease with HR 0.53 over 6 years; rates were 4.2 versus 8.0 cases of PACD per 1,000 eye years in treated and untreated eyes, respectively. These disease endpoints should not be equated with demonstrated prevention of glaucoma or severe visual impairment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People with PAC and IOP > 30mmHg; the EAGLE trial enrolled people with PAC with IOP above 30 mmHg.
decision_rules: Prefer lens extraction by phacoemulsification to laser PI for disease meeting the stated IOP criterion.
Decisions to extract a lens to control angle-closure disease should involve a consultant with a specialist interest in glaucoma.

recommended_regimens.name: Phacoemulsification lens extraction
recommended_regimens.summary: Preferred to laser PI for PAC with IOP > 30mmHg.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In EAGLE, after 3 years IOP was 1 mmHg lower with phacoemulsification than with laser PI; the proportions off medication were 60% versus 20%, and subsequent glaucoma surgery occurred in 0.5% versus 11% of the phaco and laser PI groups, respectively. The trial also reported better patient-reported and economic outcomes with phacoemulsification.

not_recommended.name: Goniosynechialysis
not_recommended.reason: Trials found no additional benefit when it was added to phacoemulsification.

response_assessment.method: IOP, medication use and subsequent glaucoma surgery
response_assessment.interpretation: These were outcomes reported for the phacoemulsification and laser PI groups in EAGLE.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The implications of EAGLE for non-Chinese/non-European populations are uncertain. Its lens-extraction results do not justify surgery for everyone with narrow angles.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People with PACG, particularly mild to moderate disease; clear lens extraction can be considered initially for patients over 50 years of age.
decision_rules: Advise clear lens phacoemulsification as the primary intervention rather than PI.
In early to moderate PACG with co-existing cataract, use lens extraction as the initial treatment option.
Involve a consultant with a specialist interest in glaucoma in decisions to extract the lens for angle-closure control.

recommended_regimens.name: Clear lens phaco
recommended_regimens.summary: Preferred as the initial intervention for PACG over PI.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In EAGLE, after 3 years IOP was 1 mmHg lower in the phaco group, the proportions off medication were 60% versus 20%, and subsequent glaucoma surgery occurred in 0.5% versus 11% of the phaco and laser PI groups, respectively.

recommended_regimens.name: Phacoemulsification clear lens extraction/cataract surgery
recommended_regimens.summary: Preferred on safety grounds to trabeculectomy or phaco-trab for PACG, although glaucoma surgery may be considered for severe disease.

alternative_regimens.name: trabeculectomy
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered when PACG is severe.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Severe disease may warrant a glaucoma operation instead of lens extraction alone.

alternative_regimens.name: phacotrabeculectomy
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered in severe PACG.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The relative merits of sequential surgery and combined surgery in more severe or advanced disease remain unclear.

not_recommended.name: Goniosynechialysis
not_recommended.reason: Its addition to phacoemulsification has not shown supplementary benefit; phacoemulsification and GSL did not reduce the need for antiglaucoma eyedrops compared with phacoemulsification alone.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Lens extraction in these eyes can be more complicated during and after surgery than routine lens extraction. EAGLE was conducted in the UK and East Asia, so its implications for non-Chinese/non-European populations are uncertain.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People with PACG and cataract whose IOP is medically controlled.
decision_rules: Use phacoemulsification alone as an initial surgical option; weigh any reduction in medication use from combined surgery against its greater complication burden.

recommended_regimens.name: phacoemulsification alone
recommended_regimens.summary: An effective option for PACG with co-existing cataract and medically controlled IOP.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A cited randomised study found reduced IOP and postoperative glaucoma medication requirements at 2 years. It found no significant between-group differences in IOP, visual acuity or visual-field progression compared with phaco-trabeculectomy with mitomycin-C; the combined-surgery group used fewer topical medications during the 2-year period but experienced more complications.

alternative_regimens.name: phaco-trabeculectomy with mitomycin-C
alternative_regimens.summary: In a cited randomised study it reduced topical medication use more than phacoemulsification alone but caused more complications.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The guide does not establish a preferred circumstance for choosing combined surgery in medically controlled disease.

response_assessment.method: IOP, medication requirements, visual acuity, visual-field progression and complications
response_assessment.interpretation: These outcomes were compared in the cited study of phacoemulsification alone and combined surgery.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People with medically uncontrolled PACG and co-existing cataract, including those with advanced disease.
decision_rules: Consider the severity of glaucoma and the sequence of lens and glaucoma surgery carefully.
For advanced PACG with uncontrolled IOP and cataract, primary trabeculectomy with mitomycin-C may be viable.

alternative_regimens.name: phaco-trabeculectomy with mitomycin-C
alternative_regimens.summary: In a cited study of medically uncontrolled PACG with cataract, combined surgery produced lower postoperative IOP and less glaucoma medication use than phacoemulsification alone over the 2-year follow-up period, but caused more complications.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider when control of IOP requires more than lens extraction alone; benefits relative to sequential surgery in more severe disease remain unclear.

alternative_regimens.name: primary trabeculectomy with mitomycin-C
alternative_regimens.summary: May be a viable operation in advanced PACG with uncontrolled IOP and concurrent cataract.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Advanced disease with uncontrolled IOP.

response_assessment.method: Postoperative IOP, glaucoma medication use and complications
response_assessment.interpretation: The cited comparison found lower IOP and medication use, but more complications, after phaco-trabeculectomy than after phacoemulsification alone.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The benefits of sequential cataract and glaucoma operations versus combined phaco-trabeculectomy in more severe or advanced disease remain unclear.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People with medically uncontrolled PACG without cataract, particularly younger patients who retain accommodative ability.
decision_rules: Consider trabeculectomy with mitomycin C while accounting for its higher surgical complication burden and subsequent cataract risk.

alternative_regimens.name: trabeculectomy with mitomycin C
alternative_regimens.summary: May be indicated for uncontrolled PACG without cataract, especially in younger patients with accommodation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: IOP remains medically uncontrolled and the lens is clear.

alternative_regimens.name: phacoemulsification
alternative_regimens.summary: Was the comparator in a small randomised trial involving medically uncontrolled PACG with clear lenses.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The guide does not specify a preference for it over trabeculectomy in this population.

response_assessment.method: Medication requirements, surgical complications, additional surgery and cataract development
response_assessment.interpretation: In the cited small trial, the trabeculectomy group required on average 1.1 fewer drugs after surgery; complications occurred in 44% versus 4% of trabeculectomy and phacoemulsification patients, respectively. Additional surgical interventions did not differ between groups at 2 years, while one third of trabeculectomy patients developed significant cataract within that period.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Suggested trabeculectomy modifications include a more anterior sclerostomy, measures to maintain a deep anterior chamber and avoid major intraoperative IOP fluctuations, and postoperative measures to limit hypotony.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People requiring medication to lower IOP in PACG, including eyes after LPI.
decision_rules: Prostaglandin monotherapy lowers IOP more effectively than timolol monotherapy in the evidence cited for PACG after LPI.
The guide does not establish an advantage of one PGA over another.

recommended_regimens.name: Prostaglandin monotherapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Effective for IOP reduction in PACG and more effective than timolol.

alternative_regimens.name: beta blockers
alternative_regimens.summary: Included among the medical treatment classes used for PACG.

alternative_regimens.name: alpha-agonists
alternative_regimens.summary: Included among the medical treatment classes used for PACG.

alternative_regimens.name: carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
alternative_regimens.summary: Included among the medical treatment classes used for PACG.

alternative_regimens.name: pilocarpine
alternative_regimens.summary: May help in PACG with a non-pupil-block or plateau iris mechanism, but is not used extensively because of its adverse-effect profile.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A non-pupil-block or plateau iris mechanism.

response_assessment.interpretation: Assess pressure reduction with medical treatment.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guide reports no benefit of one PGA over another (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak).

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People presenting with acute primary angle closure caused by pupillary block or plateau iris, after exclusion of lenticular and retro-lenticular secondary mechanisms.
decision_rules: Promptly confirm angle closure and raised IOP, identify or exclude secondary causes, and check for prior medication allergies or contraindications.
Give immediate pressure-lowering treatment, then perform laser peripheral iridotomy as quickly as technically feasible.

Before systemic acetazolamide, establish whether there is a history of sulphonamide medication allergy or severe nephropathy. Treat angina due to coronary artery disease, previous myocardial infarction and prior coronary artery stenting as contraindications to apraclonidine or brimonidine.
If IOP> 40 mmHg, defer the initial G. Pilocarpine 2% and give IV Acetazolamide 250mg as specified by the acute care pathway.

recommended_regimens.name: systemic acetazolamide, topical pilocarpine and other ocular hypotensive medication
recommended_regimens.summary: Give together immediately for acute primary angle closure. The pathway specifies initial G. Dorzolamide 2%/G. Timolol 0.5% combination, G. Apraclonidine 0.5%, G. Pilocarpine 2% subject to the IOP restriction, and IV Acetazolamide 250mg if IOP> 40mmHg.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: After an initial instillation of pilocarpine, every six hours is described as an appropriate frequency; intensive pilocarpine is not advised.

recommended_regimens.name: laser peripheral iridotomy
recommended_regimens.summary: Attempt promptly in both eyes once the attack permits treatment; the acute pathway proceeds when the cornea is clear and the patient is comfortable.

recommended_regimens.name: G. Dexamethasone 0.1% or G. Prednisolone 1%
recommended_regimens.summary: Start intensive topical anti-inflammatory treatment after PI is complete.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: At minimum of hourly while awake for 24 hours then 4 x day for one week.

alternative_regimens.name: surgical iridectomy
alternative_regimens.summary: May be attempted in both eyes after the initial acute attack resolves.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An alternative to laser iridotomy following resolution of the initial attack.

not_recommended.name: Intensive pilocarpine drops
not_recommended.reason: The guide advises against intensive administration and instead describes dosing every six hours after the initial instillation.

not_recommended.name: Emergency trabeculectomy
not_recommended.reason: The guide advises against its use during the acute crisis.

not_recommended.name: Paracentesis
not_recommended.reason: It has no proven role in acute angle closure and may cause harm.

response_assessment.interpretation: Determine whether the patient and cornea permit laser peripheral iridotomy.

response_assessment.method: Assess response to medication and technical feasibility of iridotomy
response_assessment.interpretation: No or inadequate response, or a cornea that prevents iridotomy, prompts consideration of additional laser treatment.

supportive_care: Provide analgesia and anti-emesis when required.
Give topical steroids and oral analgesia and antiemetics as required during initial management.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Secondary lenticular or retro-lenticular mechanisms require a different initial approach: pilocarpine can aggravate them.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People whose acute attack has not responded sufficiently to initial medication or for whom corneal oedema makes laser iridotomy technically impossible.
decision_rules: Consider laser peripheral iridoplasty if medication has not broken the attack by 2 hours or if a hazy cornea prevents iridotomy.
Iridoplasty does not replace iridotomy as the main intervention for angle closure.

alternative_regimens.name: Argon/green laser iridoplasty
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider when initial medical treatment fails. A cited randomised trial found faster early IOP reduction with iridoplasty than with topical pilocarpine and timolol after systemic acetazolamide, but no difference between groups by two hours.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Inadequate response to topical medication and systemic acetazolamide after two hours, or a cornea too hazy for iridotomy.

response_assessment.method: IOP response and feasibility of laser iridotomy
response_assessment.interpretation: The cited trial found no difference between the iridoplasty and medication groups by this timepoint; persisting inadequate control may require further treatment.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guide reports no clear consensus on using laser iridoplasty immediately in acute angle closure.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People whose acute angle closure remains refractory to medical treatment and laser peripheral iridoplasty.
decision_rules: Consider diode laser treatment if medication and laser peripheral iridoplasty fail to control IOP.

alternative_regimens.name: Cyclodiode laser
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider for acute cases refractory to both medication and ALPI.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Persistent attack despite medical therapy and ALPI.

alternative_regimens.name: diode laser cycloablation
alternative_regimens.summary: Described as frequently effective for controlling IOP when medication and laser iridoplasty have failed.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Continuing IOP elevation after the preceding treatments.

not_recommended.name: Emergency trabeculectomy
not_recommended.reason: The guide advises against emergency use.

not_recommended.name: Limbal paracentesis
not_recommended.reason: Although rapid IOP reduction has been reported, the guide notes anecdotal severe complications and states that paracentesis has no proven role and may cause harm.

response_assessment.interpretation: Determine whether pressure is controlled after escalation.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The acute care pathway recommends that NHS eye departments providing urgent care have diode laser capability.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: The contralateral eye of a person who has experienced acute symptomatic angle closure.
decision_rules: Attempt preventive laser iridotomy in the fellow eye without delay, when the acute attack is treated and before discharge once IOP is controlled.

recommended_regimens.name: Laser iridotomy
recommended_regimens.summary: Recommended for every contralateral eye after an acute symptomatic attack in the other eye.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Laser iridotomy appears to prevent long-term IOP rises in around 90% of these fellow eyes.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: At the time when the acute angle-closure is treated.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guide regards fellow-eye treatment as necessary despite noting that this specific preventive approach has not been tested in an RCT.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People with cataract who have had an acute angle-closure episode, after IOP control and clearing of the cornea.
decision_rules: Offer early phacoemulsification once IOP is controlled and the cornea is clear.
Early phaco may offer more benefit than PI in AAC with cataract.

recommended_regimens.name: phacoemulsification
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer early lens surgery after stabilisation of an acute attack in a patient with cataract.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a cited randomised trial enrolling people with AAC, cataract and visual acuity of ≤6/15 whose IOP reached ≤30 mmHg within 24 hours on medication, 2-year cumulative survival was 61% after LPI and 89% after phaco/IOL (P = 0.034). The authors interpreted this as suggesting that phaco/IOL may stabilise IOP better.

alternative_regimens.name: laser peripheral iridotomy
alternative_regimens.summary: The comparison treatment in the cited randomised trial.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The guide does not specify when to prefer it over early phacoemulsification in this cataract population.

response_assessment.interpretation: The cited trial enrolled patients whose IOP was ≤30 mmHg within this period.
The cited trial reported 61% for LPI and 89% for phaco/IOL (P = 0.034).

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: A separate surgery recommendation states that early phaco may offer more benefit than PI for AAC and PACG with cataract (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak).

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People with residual iridotrabecular contact (ITC) after laser PI, without another indication for intervention.
decision_rules: Do not intervene further for ITC alone; use IOP, glaucoma status, visual function in both eyes and any recurrent symptoms to guide management.
Consider residual ITC when determining follow-up intensity.
Consider an additional intervention only if IOP rises, GON worsens or symptomatic attacks recur.

not_recommended.name: Additional interventions for ITC alone
not_recommended.reason: Evidence does not support treatment solely because iridotrabecular contact persists.

not_recommended.name: Laser peripheral iridoplasty
not_recommended.reason: Trials found no IOP-lowering benefit from adding it to laser iridotomy in PAC/PACG.

response_assessment.method: IOP, evidence of GON progression, recurrent symptomatic attacks and visual function of both eyes
response_assessment.interpretation: A documented change in these findings, rather than residual ITC alone, may justify further intervention.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guide reports non-synechial residual ITC in between 20% and 33% of cases after laser peripheral iridotomy and notes that it is rarely seen after phacoemulsification.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People with PAC or PACG whose angle opens after iridotomy, or people with PACG being considered for further laser or minimally invasive procedures.
decision_rules: Do not use laser trabeculoplasty as a treatment for PAC or PACG.
Do not infer an established role for MIGS, non-penetrating surgery or additional laser approaches where effectiveness remains unproven.

alternative_regimens.name: Glaucoma drainage device (GDD) surgery
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered if the anterior chamber is sufficiently deep.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: In pseudophakic eyes with a shallow chamber, the guide describes tube placement in the ciliary sulcus; comparative evidence against trabeculectomy in PACG is lacking.

not_recommended.name: Laser trabeculoplasty
not_recommended.reason: Long-term success is generally poor, and the guide does not recommend it for any form of PAC or PACG.

not_recommended.name: Laser peripheral iridoplasty in addition to PI
not_recommended.reason: It offers no clear additional benefit in PACG and has not shown an IOP-lowering benefit.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: MIGS devices are not licensed for angle-closure glaucoma in the UK, and their effectiveness in angle-closure disease remains insufficiently proven. Evidence for non-penetrating surgery is not useful; evidence supporting micropulse TSCPC or endoscopic cyclophotocoagulation for PACG is lacking. SLT after PI offers no clear IOP-control benefit (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak).

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People with angle-closure disease and visually significant cataract.
decision_rules: Offer cataract treatment in accordance with current cataract surgery guidance.
Do not make laser iridotomy a routine prerequisite to phacoemulsification and IOL.
When pressure instability is documented or intermittent symptomatic angle closure is suspected, dilate immediately before surgery without an undue wait.

recommended_regimens.name: Phacoemulsification and IOL
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer lens surgery in line with cataract guidance when cataract is visually significant.

not_recommended.name: Routine laser peripheral iridotomy prior to phacoemulsification and IOL
not_recommended.reason: Evidence does not support routinely performing this preliminary procedure (Evidence/recommendation: Low; Weak).

response_assessment.method: Axial-length biometry and assessment of ocular comorbidity
response_assessment.interpretation: Short axial length affects complication risk and the accuracy of ocular biometry; comorbid conditions may limit visual prognosis.

supportive_care: Discuss and document excess surgical risk when axial length is < 21.00.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guide states that below 21mm axial length, complications double with every 1 mm reduction in axial length. It also notes that biometry in very small eyes is less accurate and that amblyopia or foveal hypoplasia may limit visual outcomes. Cases of angle closure are not recommended for early years trainee surgeons.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People with eyes measuring less than 20.00 mm in axial length who are undergoing lens or cataract extraction.
decision_rules: Counsel about the increased complication risk and possible refractive surprise before surgery.
Consider surgical iridectomy during lens extraction to reduce postoperative pupil block risk and facilitate management should aqueous misdirection occur.
For very small eyes with very shallow anterior chambers, consider concurrent pars plana vitrectomy after discussion with a vitreo-retinal surgeon.

alternative_regimens.name: surgical iridectomy
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider performing it during lens or cataract extraction to reduce postoperative pupil block and assist with any subsequent aqueous misdirection.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An eye with nanophthalmos undergoing lens or cataract surgery.

alternative_regimens.name: pars plana vitrectomy
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider at the same time as phacoemulsification after discussion with a vitreo-retinal surgeon.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A very small eye with a very shallow anterior chamber.

response_assessment.method: Biometry and counselling about complications, refractive outcome and expected visual acuity
response_assessment.interpretation: Accurate biometry is challenging; underlying amblyopia or foveal hypoplasia may limit the visual result.

supportive_care: Explain that lens or cataract surgery complications may occur in 30% of cases or more; the examples listed are aqueous misdirection, zonular dialysis, cystoid macular oedema and choroidal effusions.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guide states that a significant proportion may not achieve BCVA > 6/12 because of underlying amblyopia or foveal hypoplasia (Evidence/recommendation: Low; Weak). Counselling on complication and refractive risks is graded Moderate; Strong.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People with suspected aqueous misdirection, especially after surgery and with sudden anterior-chamber shallowing; IOP may be normal.
decision_rules: Begin with cycloplegia and suppression of aqueous production, add a hyperosmotic agent if appropriate, and ensure a patent peripheral iridotomy.
Account for contraindications before using mannitol.

recommended_regimens.name: atropine or cyclopentolate
recommended_regimens.summary: Use as initial cycloplegic treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: aqueous production suppressants
recommended_regimens.summary: Give systemically and/or topically as part of initial medical treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: mannitol
recommended_regimens.summary: A subsequent hyperosmotic treatment option when not contraindicated.

recommended_regimens.name: peripheral iridotomy
recommended_regimens.summary: Perform if a patent iridotomy is not already present.

response_assessment.interpretation: A normal IOP does not exclude aqueous misdirection.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Short axial length, an angle-closure diagnosis and phakic lens status are listed as risk factors. The guide states that good evidence for prevention and management is lacking.

In pseudophakic eyes, Nd:YAG laser vitreolysis/capsulotomy may be tried.
Consider the described zonulo-hyaloido-vitrectomy approaches or diode laser cyclophotocoagulation as further options.

Dilate the pupil rather than treating initially with pilocarpine.
Direct subsequent care at the underlying lenticular pathology.

Use cycloplegia or pupil dilation initially rather than pilocarpine, and direct further treatment at the underlying pathology.
