document_sections.heading: 1.1 Background
document_sections.content: Glaucoma affects an estimated 80 million people worldwide and is a major cause of blindness. It is an intermittently progressive optic neuropathy that produces visual field defects attributable to injury at the pre-laminar optic nerve head. Lowering intraocular pressure slows or stops progression in the vast majority of cases. Secondary glaucoma arises from another ocular or systemic disorder, commonly neovascularization, uveitis or ocular trauma, and typically causes a marked pressure rise. Primary glaucoma has no such precipitating disease. Primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG) and primary open angle glaucoma (POAG) are distinguished by whether the iris obstructs the iridocorneal drainage angle. They differ in presentation and treatment; PACG depends more strongly on pressure, and its treatment aims to remove barriers to aqueous circulation. In primary angle-closure suspects (PACS), the iris contacts the trabecular meshwork, but intraocular pressure (IOP), optic nerve structure and visual function remain normal, without peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS). Primary angle-closure (PAC) involves current or previous IOP elevation and/or PAS, without glaucomatous optic nerve injury or visual field abnormality. PACG can arise without previously detected high IOP or PAS. Acute angle-closure (AAC) occurs when sudden complete trabecular obstruction produces extreme ocular hypertension; pain, abrupt visual reduction or loss, nausea and/or vomiting may be severe. Prompt presentation and suitable treatment have improved its outlook. PACG causes severe visual loss more often than POAG: approximately 60 million people worldwide have POAG versus 20 million with PACG, yet the numbers blinded by the two conditions are roughly equal. This greater threat has encouraged consideration of prevention.

document_sections.heading: 1.3 Current practice, and why there is scope for change
document_sections.content: Angle-closure glaucoma chiefly affects older people. PACG is uncommon in adults under 40; when present at that age, plateau iris is thought to predominate. Cases in children are documented but very rare. Angle-closure occurs at approximately a 3:1 female-to-male ratio. Asian heritage carries a greater burden; acute angle-closure incidence in Chinese patients is three-fold that in Caucasians, while angle-closure glaucoma is uncommon among Africans. The ICD10 table identifies codes for PACS, PAC, PACG and its acute, chronic, intermittent and residual forms, as well as drug-related glaucoma, aqueous misdirection, plateau iris syndrome and adverse effects of ophthalmological preparations. Surgical iridectomy entered glaucoma treatment in September 1857 and remained central until laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) superseded it in the mid 1970’s. LPI has also become a preventive intervention; prevention in the fellow eye after an acute crisis has an unquestioned role. EAGLE, reported in 2016, compared LPI with clear lens phacoemulsification in PAC with IOP above 30 mmHg or PACG. For patients meeting its entry criteria, lens extraction was generally safe, effective and cost-effective, and improved quality of life relative to LPI, prompting a shift away from LPI in PAC and PACG. Preventive LPI for asymptomatic people without documented pressure elevation remains common despite lacking a firm evidence base. Around 75% of UK ophthalmology consultants offer it for narrow or occluded angles. England's NHS recorded 13,844 patient episodes whose primary procedure was LPI in 2018-19; most likely involved prophylaxis, creating a substantial capacity burden. Pressures on the NHS during the first six months of 2020 further motivated reassessment of established practice.

document_sections.heading: 2.1 Main Aims
document_sections.content: The guideline addresses primary angle-closure across its disease spectrum and excludes secondary forms caused by conditions such as uveitis or neovascularization. It is primarily for clinicians providing community or hospital eye care. Its 4 aims concern diagnostic test accuracy, intervention effectiveness, referral to hospital eye services and discharge to community care.

document_sections.heading: 2.2 Key Clinical questions Epidemiology
document_sections.content: The questions cover classification and natural history of the primary angle-closure spectrum; prevalence and PACG-related visual morbidity in the UK, or in European or White US populations where UK evidence is limited; and established PACG risk factors. Diagnostic questions address suitable tests in secondary and tertiary care, provocative testing, and case detection in optometry or primary care. Management questions address preventive iridotomy, including fellow-eye prophylaxis after AAC; acute-crisis care; established PACG; relevant systematic reviews and meta-analyses; laser, medical and surgical interventions; and whether care should vary by racial group. Follow-up questions concern residual iridotrabecular contact (ITC), cataract management including whether LPI should precede phacoemulsification, and pupil dilation in suspected or established angle-closure.

document_sections.heading: 3.1 Search strategy
document_sections.content: Questions were structured with PICO. A systematic literature review used searches developed with the Cochrane Eyes and Vision Group. Medline, Embase and the Cochrane Library were searched for publications between 2000 & 2017, alongside website searches including the US National Guidelines Clearinghouse. The guideline development group evaluated selected publications with standard checklists before accepting conclusions as evidence. Eligible evidence types included published guidelines, systematic reviews, randomised controlled trials, cohort and case-control studies, and case series. Non-English papers, conference abstracts and letters were excluded.

document_sections.heading: 3.2 Evidence and grading
document_sections.content: Evidence quality and recommendation strength follow the GRADE Working Group system. High means further research is very unlikely to change confidence in an effect estimate; Moderate means research is likely to affect confidence substantially and might change the estimate; Low means research is very likely to affect confidence substantially and probably change the estimate; and Very low means any estimate is highly uncertain. Strong denotes an action or avoidance that most well-informed people would choose. Weak denotes a choice favoured by a majority of well-informed people, although a substantial minority would choose otherwise.

document_sections.heading: 4.1 Terminology & Disease Definitions
document_sections.content: Primary angle-closure requires iris–trabecular meshwork contact without another causative ocular or systemic disease. This primary irido-trabecular contact (ITC) may raise intraocular pressure (IOP), potentially causing glaucomatous sight loss; cataract or retinal vascular disease can also impair vision. Glaucoma involves retinal ganglion cell axon injury at the pre-laminar optic nerve head with reproducible visual field loss, and lowering IOP slows or stops it. PACG combines structural optic nerve damage and lost visual function with an occluded drainage angle, with elevated IOP presumed to mediate the injury. Other explanations for visual loss should be considered and investigated when needed. Acute angle-closure is an ophthalmic emergency: profound, abrupt ocular hypertension and its treatment can leave patients seriously ill. Symptomatic patients tend to present earlier in the disease course than asymptomatic patients; over longer follow-up, 9% become blind from glaucoma, and a similar proportion have reportedly lost sight from unoperated cataract. Older symptom-based classifications into acute, subacute and chronic forms are limited because blurring, haloes and periocular pain also occur frequently in people without angle-closure. The terms narrow angle and narrow angle glaucoma are misleading when applied to eyes without ITC and can expose people with little meaningful angle-closure-related visual risk to unnecessary treatment or monitoring. Classification should instead reflect physical signs pertinent to current visual function or future visual prognosis. The prognostic importance of peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) remains uncertain. Natural-history stage and the likely site of aqueous-flow obstruction provide complementary classification frameworks.

document_sections.heading: Natural History Staging of Angle-closure Disease5
document_sections.content: Primary angle closure suspect denotes ITC with normal IOP and no glaucomatous optic neuropathy. In primary angle closure, IOP is elevated without glaucomatous optic neuropathy; lens opacity or retinal vascular pathology may coexist. Acute angle closure (AAC) crisis warrants rapid care distinct from routine management. Its post-crisis physical signs do not invariably determine long-term vision, although often-reversible current impairment may arise from lens opacity or an unresponsive dilated pupil following iris ischemia. Glaucomatous optic neuropathy at an acute presentation probably predates, rather than results from, a pressure elevation lasting hours or days. Primary angle closure glaucoma is the stage with glaucomatous optic neuropathy in an occluded-angle eye, defined by pre-laminar optic nerve head structural changes together with reproducible visual field loss.

document_sections.heading: Underlying mechanism of angle closure
document_sections.content: Anatomical classification places aqueous-flow obstruction at the pupil, ciliary body, lens or behind the lens in the vitreous or retina; clinically, distinguishing anterior pupil or ciliary-body obstruction from posterior lenticular or retro-lenticular obstruction is particularly important. Pupil block accounts primarily for 75% of cases, so iridotomy may control earlier disease. Because pupil block can coexist with plateau iris, laser iridotomy merits consideration even when another mechanism is suspected. The designation lens-induced glaucoma is best restricted to a white, intumescent or unstable lens. In UK angle-closure presentations, lenticular block accounts for approximately 5% and retro-lenticular block for approximately 1%. Unlike pupil block and anterior non-pupil-block mechanisms, which initially respond well to pilocarpine, these less-common posterior mechanisms are typically worsened by pilocarpine. Cycloplegia with cyclopentolate or atropine is effective initial medical treatment for them.

document_sections.heading: 4.2 Epidemiology
document_sections.content: A systematic review estimated PACG in 0.4% of white European adults aged over 40, corresponding to 130,000 people in the UK and 1.6 million across Europe. Demographic projections suggest prevalence might rise by 20% per decade as life expectancy increases. European POAG prevalence is around 2.5%; PACG may represent approximately one case in 6 of UK glaucoma. Evidence about PACG-related visual morbidity in white Europeans is limited and of low quality. A review of worldwide prevalence studies projected 5.3 million people with bilateral severe visual impairment from PACG in 2020, against 5.9 million people blinded globally by POAG. Shallow central and peripheral anterior chambers are consistently identified as risks for primary angle-closure disease, PACG and acute crises. Short axial length and thicker, more anterior lenses are plausible but less firmly established risks. Hypermetropic refraction is associated with angle-closure inconsistently; myopic people can also be affected, so refractive error should not determine who receives risk assessment. Occluded angles are heritable. Genome-wide association studies link several single nucleotide polymorphisms with increased risk; COL11A1 increases angle-closure disease risk, and SPATA13 mutations have been linked with familial cases among white UK citizens and identified as the first causative gene. Overt secondary angle-closure in Marfan/Weill Marchesani syndrome and Ehler-Danlos syndrome supports a relationship with abnormal ocular connective tissue. Retinitis Pigmentosa and Best Vitelliform Macular Dystrophy are also associated with angle-closure. When PACG or AAC is newly identified, relatives should be informed about NHS sight-testing guidance; first-degree relatives with potentially occluded angles found at testing should be referred. First-degree relatives of patients with significant primary angle-closure disease, excluding PACS alone, should receive regular community optometric review and, if current referral criteria are met, hospital assessment for possible preventive laser iridotomy. Research should compare ways to identify occluded angles in first-degree relatives, including community case-finding and direct hospital referral. Incident AAC rates reported for European populations are 2 – 5 /100,000/year, compared with 12 – 16/100,000/year in Chinese populations and 6 – 7 /100,000/year in South and Southeast Asian populations; these reports generally concern people aged 30 years and older and may be biased by reliance on hospital episodes. A Chinese prophylactic-iridotomy trial reported 8 new cases/1,000 years in untreated PACS eyes (36/889 eyes over 6 years follow-up). New PAS was most frequent (30/889 eyes); elevated IOP and acute crises were each reported in 5/889 eyes, and Three eyes met IOP and PAS endpoints simultaneously. No incident glaucomatous optic neuropathy arose over the six-year follow-up period. Thus progression, particularly vision-threatening progression, was uncommon even in this high-risk population. Approximately 1/1000 per year is presented as a memorable AAC risk for patients with narrow or occluded angles; incidence data suggest the true risk in the white UK population may be lower by a factor of 3 or 4. For otherwise uncomplicated PACS with occluded angles, incident sight-threatening symptomatic or asymptomatic disease risk is less than 1/1000 per year (Evidence/recommendation: High; Strong).

document_sections.heading: 4.3 Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Gonioscopy is the principal diagnostic and monitoring examination for primary angle-closure; dynamic assessment reveals drainage-angle anatomy unavailable through other techniques. It may be uncomfortable, requires training and practice, and can take considerable time in established disease. Limbal anterior chamber depth (LACD), or the van Herick test, is a quick non-contact adjunct to gonioscopy that staff can learn and perform in primary and secondary care. High frequency ultrasound biomicroscopy and anterior segment OCT (AS OCT) add anatomical imaging and may yield measurements useful for future risk assessment. AS OCT can rapidly document the angle without contact, support remote review and audit, and, under lower-light conditions, disclose previously unrecognized angle-closure. Identifying the scleral spur or Schwalbe’s line can limit its ability to establish ITC. AS OCT generally detects more ITC than gonioscopy; some studies find LACD and AS OCT more consistent than gonioscopy for identifying at-risk people, but the significance is unproven. AS OCT can document angle-width changes before and after PI and assist discussion with patients. No anterior-segment imaging or biometry method has been proven to identify who will later develop glaucoma. A Cochrane review judged evidence on LACD and AS-OCT diagnostic performance sub-optimal; pooled LACD data indicated high sensitivity and sufficient specificity for case-finding, with performance comparable to more complex imaging, while highlighting the need for better studies. Gonioscopy remains definitive for diagnosis and surveillance; AS OCT supplements rather than replaces it, particularly because it cannot detect PAS in place of gonioscopy. PAS-related visual prognosis remains unclear. Longitudinal research is needed to validate AS OCT measurements for diagnosis, prognosis, progression prediction and intervention assessment. In secondary care, AS-OCT may help triage referrals and avoid some gonioscopy examinations. There is no evidence supporting provocative tests for PAC/PACG diagnosis or monitoring (Evidence/recommendation: High; Strong).

document_sections.heading: t. Should provocative tests be used?
document_sections.content: Because pharmacological dilation is associated with symptomatic ocular hypertension in angle-closure, it has been considered as a way to identify higher-risk individuals. Other proposed provocations include face-down positioning, darkness and their combination. Combined pilocarpine and phenylephrine aims to maintain a mid-dilated pupil, thought to carry particularly high pressure-rise risk. Provocative testing is controversial and lacks evidence of consistently identifying people at substantial risk. A randomised nested ZAP study found that a brief dark-prone test did not identify participants who subsequently reached a trial endpoint. Provocative tests are therefore not currently recommended.

document_sections.heading: u. What are the recommended tests for case detection in community and primary care
document_sections.content: Historically, community optometrists and primary care practitioners referred suspected angle-closure, including PACS identified solely by an occludable angle despite normal IOP, optic disc and visual fields. Community tests should be quick, straightforward and cost neutral. A Cochrane review examined the oblique flashlight test, LACD, AS-OCT, Scheimpflug photography and scanning peripheral anterior chamber depth analyser (SPAC). Despite sub-optimal study quality, it found high sensitivity and specificity for the simple LACD assessment and suggested possible targeted screening in high-prevalence populations. Available AS OCT is a useful supplement because its image record can be sent for referral triage. Given the low visual-loss risk with isolated occluded angles, referrals should follow NICE guidance for elevated IOP or glaucoma. Without those indications, presumed occluded angles warrant referral when PACS PLUS criteria apply: limbal chamber depth grade < ¼ or AS OCT-demonstrated ITC, together with at least one added factor. Those factors are only one “good eye” whose deterioration could threaten independence or livelihood; a vulnerable adult potentially unable to report symptoms; family history of significant angle-closure disease; hypermetropia > + 6.00 dioptres; diabetes or another need for repeated dilation; antidepressant or anticholinergic medication; or residence or work in a remote place without prompt emergency ophthalmic care. PACS PLUS warrants Hospital Eye Service referral. Someone meeting the angle criterion but no added criterion or NICE glaucoma referral indication should instead be advised to have an annual NHS sight test.

document_sections.heading: 4.4 Management
document_sections.content: In the 2016 EAGLE randomised controlled trial, people with PACG regardless of IOP, or PAC with IOP >/= 30 mmHg, received clear lens phacoemulsification or laser iridotomy. Phacoemulsification performed better on disease-control, economic and patient-reported measures. At 3 years, IOP in the phaco group was 1 mmHg lower, while 60% versus 20% of the two respective groups were off medication and subsequent glaucoma surgery occurred in 0.5% vs 11% of the phaco and laser PI groups, respectively. Economic modelling found cost savings; quality of life stayed stable with phacoemulsification but declined with LPI. RCTs found no supplementary benefit from goniosynechiolysis (GSL) alongside phacoemulsification. LPI effectiveness may decline as severity increases: most PACS eyes needed no further treatment, whereas many PAC, PACG and acute PAC eyes required additional IOP control. Trials gave conflicting dysphotopsia findings for temporal versus other iridotomy sites; no consistent site effect is established. Bleeding rates appear unchanged when anticoagulants are continued if INR remains below 3.0. Two RCT’s found no extra IOP benefit from laser peripheral iridoplasty alongside LPI in PAC/PACG. Lens extraction by phacoemulsification is preferred to laser PI for PAC with IOP > 30mmHg (Evidence/recommendation: High; Strong). Goniosynechialysis should not be performed because benefit has not been shown (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak). Anticoagulants need not be stopped for PI when INR < 3 (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak). PI can be superior (12 o’clock) or temporal because consistent evidence of a dysphotopsia difference is lacking (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak). Residual ITC after PI is described in 20-80% of cases; ITC alone does not justify another intervention, although it can inform follow-up risk stratification (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak). Laser peripheral iridoplasty has shown no IOP-lowering benefit in this setting (Evidence/recommendation: High; Strong).

document_sections.heading: w. When to do a laser iridotomy in narrow angles/occludable angles/PACS
document_sections.content: A Mongolian screening RCT (N= 4,725) compared no intervention with anterior-chamber-depth screening followed by an offer of iridotomy to participants meeting PACS criteria. Incident glaucoma did not differ, and the study concluded that population-wide screening and prophylaxis for higher-risk people offered no benefit. ZAP screened 11,991 people over 50 in southern China and identified 889 with PACS; one eye received LPI and the other remained untreated. LPI halved new angle-closure disease risk (HR 0.53 over 6 years), but treated and untreated rates were only 4.2 versus 8.0 cases of PACD per 1,000 eye years. Most endpoints were new PAS with little immediate apparent visual threat. The number needed to treat to prevent PAC was 44 over 6 years; neither incident glaucoma nor severe visual impairment occurred. Extrapolation using available data projected treatment of 126 people to prevent one glaucoma case over 10 years. Applicability to nonChinese populations is unproven, although UK risk is reasonably assumed no higher than in this older, high-risk Chinese population. On present medical evidence, routine prophylactic LPI for all PACS is not advised; high-risk PACS may benefit. UK economic extrapolation and the Singapore ANALIS study were still underway, with preliminary ANALIS findings pointing toward similar outcomes to ZAP. Familial clustering is suggested by heritability and genetic studies, but whether relatives have greater glaucoma risk has not been directly investigated. Regular pharmacological dilation for retinal disease increases AAC risk. Research is needed on whether PAS predicts sight loss and whether family history or known genetic risk variants raise the risk of glaucoma-related visual loss. Evidence indicates no benefit from screening and prevention for PACG in a high-risk Asian population (Evidence/recommendation: High; Strong). Although preventive PI halves incident PAC disease in high-risk Chinese PACS patients over the age of 50 years, absolute risk is low, so most would gain little benefit (Evidence/recommendation: High; Strong). Until more evidence is available, PI is advised for PACS PLUS with added factors such as an only eye, relevant family history, marked hypermetropia, repeated dilation needs, antidepressant or anticholinergic use, or remote location without emergency care (Evidence/recommendation: Low; Strong). PI is not advised for most PACS without additional risks (Evidence/recommendation: High; Strong).

document_sections.heading: x. Laser iridotomy in the fellow eye of people suffering acute angle-closure
document_sections.content: The contralateral eye is at high risk after an acute attack. Laser iridotomy appears to prevent long-term IOP elevation in around 90% of fellow eyes. Despite the absence of an RCT, the guideline regards fellow-eye iridotomy as mandatory. Reports of a fellow-eye crisis within days after discharge without iridotomy support attempting it promptly, before discharge and after IOP control. Iridotomy is recommended for every contralateral eye when the first eye develops symptomatic AAC, at the time the acute episode is treated (Evidence/recommendation: Low; Strong).

document_sections.heading: y. What is the recommended management of an acute angle-closure crisis
document_sections.content: Few randomised trials provide robust evidence for acute-crisis care, but its general principles are not disputed. Moderate-to-severe pain, abrupt visual reduction, nausea and vomiting make analgesia, antiemesis and rapid diagnostic confirmation immediate priorities, followed by topical and systemic IOP-lowering treatment. Confirm angle-closure and elevated IOP and exclude secondary mechanisms. Lenticular or retro-lenticular obstruction calls for cycloplegia with atropine or cyclopentolate; pilocarpine would worsen it and delay relief. Marked asymmetry of central anterior chamber depth points toward a lenticular or retro-lenticular mechanism. In atypical cases, ask specifically about topiramate: associated supraciliary effusions and anterior ciliary-body rotation are a regularly reported cause of bilateral angle-closure from a posterior mechanism. In presumed pupil block or plateau iris, laser peripheral iridotomy is the key intervention and should be performed as quickly as possible. Intensive pilocarpine is not advised; following an initial dose, an appropriate frequency is every six hours. Systemic acetazolamide is particularly useful initially, after checking for sulphonamide-drug allergy, including trimethoprim, and severe nephropathy. Add other topical ocular hypotensives according to the circumstances and medical history, and begin intensive topical steroids. Ask about angina from coronary artery disease, previous myocardial infarction and coronary artery stenting, all considered contraindications to apraclonidine or brimonidine. An RCT comparing early laser iridoplasty with pilocarpine and timolol after systemic acetazolamide found faster initial IOP reduction with laser but no group difference by two hours. Immediate use of iridoplasty lacks clear consensus; it could be second-line after failure of topical drugs and systemic acetazolamide at two hours or when corneal haze prevents iridotomy. Diode laser cycloablation often controls pressure refractory to medication and iridoplasty. Emergency trabeculectomy is not advised. Limbal paracentesis may rapidly lower IOP, but serious complications have been reported anecdotally. In an RCT of AAC patients treated within 1 week of presentation, whose IOP reached ≤30 mmHg within 24 hours on medication and who had cataract and acuity ≤6/15, 2-year cumulative survival was 61% with LPI versus 89% with phacoemulsification and intraocular lens implantation (phaco/IOL; P = 0.034); the finding suggests phaco/IOL may stabilize pressure better. Immediately give systemic acetazolamide, topical pilocarpine and other ocular hypotensives together for acute primary angle-closure, plus topical steroids, oral analgesia and antiemetics when required. Consider argon/green laser iridoplasty if medication does not break the attack (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak), and cyclodiode laser if both medication and ALPI fail (Evidence/recommendation: Low; Strong). Attempt laser iridotomy or surgical iridectomy in both eyes after the initial attack resolves (Evidence/recommendation: Low; Strong). Paracentesis has no proven role and may cause harm (Evidence/recommendation: Low; Strong). Offer early phacoemulsification after IOP control and corneal clearing to patients with cataract and AAC, approximately 1 to 4 weeks after presentation (Evidence/recommendation: Low; Strong). Secondary lenticular or retro-lenticular cases with acute symptoms or high pressure should receive mydriasis, not pilocarpine.

document_sections.heading: Acute Angle Closure Care Pathway (pupillary block or plateau iris mechanism)
document_sections.content: Provide analgesia and antiemesis if needed; verify that angle-closure is causing raised pressure and look for lenticular, retro-lenticular and other secondary causes. Check allergies and contraindications. Initial medicines are G. Dorzolamide 2%/G. Timolol 0.5% combination, G. Apraclonidine 0.5%, G. Pilocarpine 2%* (defer if IOP> 40 mmHg), and IV Acetazolamide 250mg if IOP> 40mmHg. Review after 30-60 minutes. If the cornea is clear and the patient comfortable enough, perform laser peripheral iridotomy in both eyes. Once PI is complete, give G. Dexamethasone 0.1% or G. Prednisolone 1% at a minimum of hourly while awake for 24 hours, then 4 x day for one week. If response remains absent or insufficient by 2 hours, or oedema prevents iridotomy, consider laser peripheral iridoplasty or diode laser cycloablation; the pathway recommends diode availability in all NHS eye departments providing urgent care. Treat secondary cases according to their underlying pathology, including drug-induced uveal effusions such as topiramate, neovascular disease or uveitis. Substitute Atropine 1% for pilocarpine in lenticular or retro-lenticular cases.

document_sections.heading: 4.5 Surgery
document_sections.content: Clear lens phacoemulsification is preferred over PI as the initial PACG intervention (Evidence/recommendation: High: Strong). Adding goniosynechialysis (GSL) to phacoemulsification does not reduce antiglaucoma-drop requirements relative to phaco alone (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak). For PACG, clear lens extraction or cataract surgery is preferred to trabeculectomy and phaco-trab on safety grounds, although trabeculectomy or phacotrabeculectomy can be considered in severe disease (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak). Early phaco may offer greater benefit than PI for AAC and PACG with cataract (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak). Lens extraction is the initial option for early-to-moderate PACG with coexisting cataract. In a small RCT involving medically controlled PACG and cataract, phaco alone reduced IOP and medication use at 2 years. Compared with phacotrabeculectomy with mitomycin-C, there were no significant differences in IOP, visual acuity or visual field progression; combined surgery used fewer topical medicines over the 2-year period but caused more complications. In medically uncontrolled PACG with cataract, combined surgery produced lower postoperative IOP and medication use during 2-year follow-up, again with more complications. Clear lens extraction (CLE) can be considered initially for mild-to-moderate PACG and PAC with IOP > 30 mmHg in patients over 50 years of age. EAGLE found slightly better pressure lowering, less medication and later glaucoma surgery, improved quality of life and better cost-effectiveness with CLE than LPI. Its UK and East Asian recruitment leaves implications for non-Chinese/non-European populations uncertain, and lens extraction may be more technically and postoperatively complicated than routine surgery. For medically uncontrolled PACG without cataract, trabeculectomy with mitomycin C may be indicated, particularly in younger patients retaining accommodation. A small RCT in such eyes found trabeculectomy more effective than phacoemulsification, requiring an average of 1.1 fewer drugs, but surgical complications occurred in 44% vs. 4% respectively. Additional surgical interventions did not differ at 2 years; one third of trabeculectomy patients developed significant cataract in that period. Primary trabeculectomy with mitomycin-C may also be viable for advanced PACG with uncontrolled IOP and cataract; surgical sequencing requires care, and the relative benefits of sequential versus combined surgery remain unclear. Suggested trabeculectomy modifications include an anterior sclerostomy, maintenance of a deep anterior chamber and advance suture placement to limit intraoperative IOP fluctuations, and tight multiple scleral-flap sutures, cautious suture lysis or removal, and cycloplegia to avoid postoperative hypotony. MIGS devices are not licensed for angle-closure glaucoma in the UK; despite generally favourable safety, efficacy is inadequately established and PAS can impede implantation. Glaucoma drainage device (GDD) surgery may be considered with adequate anterior-chamber depth; in a shallow-chamber pseudophakic eye, a tube may be placed in the ciliary sulcus. Comparative evidence for GDD versus trabeculectomy in PACG is lacking.

document_sections.heading: 4.6 Laser
document_sections.content: Prompt laser PI is advised for AAC and the fellow eye (Evidence/recommendation: Low; Strong). Laser peripheral iridoplasty adds no clear benefit to PI in PACG (Evidence/recommendation: High; Strong). SLT after PI gives no clear additional IOP-control benefit (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak). PI location and size do not appear to alter dysphotopsia frequency (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak). Sequential argon/YAG PI is preferred for dark irides, including examples in people of Asian/African descent (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Strong). A Cochrane review found too little evidence to recommend iridoplasty in nonacute PAC or PACG. During an acute attack, however, iridoplasty may break ITC, either initially or after medical-treatment failure; it does not replace iridotomy as the principal intervention. Laser trabeculoplasty after iridotomy opens the angle has generally poor long-term success in PAC and PACG and is not currently recommended for either. Few studies specifically evaluate trans-scleral cyclophotocoagulation (TSCPC) or micropulse TSCPC in angle-closure. Cyclophotocoagulation is generally reserved for refractory glaucoma. Micropulse TSCPC delivers short energy bursts to the ciliary body to produce coagulating heat, but evidence of effectiveness in PACG is lacking. Evidence likewise does not support endoscopic cyclophotocoagulation for PACG. Case series suggest TSCPC can control IOP in acute attacks resistant to standard treatment.

document_sections.heading: 4.7 Medication
document_sections.content: Prostaglandin monotherapy lowers IOP effectively in PACG and performs better than timolol (Evidence/recommendation: High; Strong). Evidence indicates no advantage of one PGA over another (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak). No evidence establishes race-specific treatment differences, although clinicians should recognize differences in biometry and iris anatomy (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Strong). PACG medical treatment resembles open-angle glaucoma treatment and can include beta blockers, prostaglandin analogues, alpha-agonists and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. After LPI, studies found prostaglandin analogues more effective than timolol monotherapy for pressure reduction. Pilocarpine or another miotic may help non-pupil-block/plateau iris PACG, but adverse effects limit its use in angle-closure disease.

document_sections.heading: z. Management in different racial groups.
document_sections.content: The guideline describes different iris behaviour in blue-eyed Caucasians and brown-eyed Asian and African people. It states that the thicker, stiffer iris in Asian and African people makes trabeculectomy and postoperative management more forgiving. No race-specific pathway has been established or demonstrated through objective research. The frequency of angle-closure disease in people of African and Caribbean heritage is poorly understood, and whether racial groups need different pathways remains uncertain.

document_sections.heading: 4.8 Follow up
document_sections.content: Residual iridotrabecular contact (ITC) alone does not support another intervention, but can inform follow-up risk after PI in PAC. Additional treatment is not recommended without a documented IOP increase, worsening GON or recurrent symptomatic attacks. Offer phacoemulsification with IOL according to cataract surgery guidance. Explain excess surgical risk when axial length is < 21.00 (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Strong). Evidence does not support recommending routine laser peripheral iridotomy before phacoemulsification and IOL (Evidence/recommendation: Low; Weak). Non-synechial residual ITC occurs in between 20% and 33% of eyes after LPI and rarely after phacoemulsification. Direct evidence to guide its management is absent; decisions depend on IOP, glaucoma and visual function in both eyes.

document_sections.heading: 4.9 Management of symptomatic cataract in angle-closure
document_sections.content: Treat visually significant cataract according to current cataract-surgery guidance. Genetic findings suggest collagen abnormalities are important in PACG; connective-tissue syndromes such as Marfan and Ehler Danlos may complicate surgery. Greater hypermetropia prevalence can conceal amblyopia, while nanophthalmos may involve foveal hypoplasia, limiting visual prognosis. For axial lengths below 21mm, complication rate doubles with every 1 mm decrease; discuss and document that excess risk. Biometry is much less accurate in very small eyes, affecting IOL selection and expected refractive results. Outcomes are generally good when axial length is > 21mm without significant ocular comorbidity, but angle-closure operations are not recommended for surgeons in their early training years. Routine presurgical laser iridotomy is not recommended. With documented pressure instability or suspected intermittent symptomatic angle-closure, dilate immediately before surgery without an undue wait.

document_sections.heading: 4.10 How to handle pupil dilation in suspected or established angle-closure
document_sections.content: Acute angle-closure following dilation is uncommon in the general population (Evidence/recommendation: High; Strong). Repeated dilation for diabetic retinopathy screening may raise AAC risk in diabetic patients (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Strong). Dilated examination is important for conditions including age-related macular degeneration, retinal vascular occlusions and diabetic retinopathy. During routine examinations, AAC risk in the general adult population is somewhere between 1/5,000 and 1/10,000; benefits therefore favour continuing routine dilation for most patients. UK diabetic retinopathy screening appears to account for more AAC cases than any other identifiable health event. Its repeated examinations may create additive risk, so identifying diabetic patients at risk and arranging glaucoma-specialist assessment for possible preventive LPI probably has value. For established or probable angle-closure, most patients can safely undergo dilation with tropicamide alone and receive PO acetazolamide 250mg when leaving the department and another dose at bedtime that night, unless contraindicated. Do not use pilocarpine to reverse dilation: it may hold the pupil mid-dilated and increase angle-closure risk.

document_sections.heading: 4.11 Aqueous misdirection/malignant glaucoma – diagnosis, prevention, management
document_sections.content: Consider aqueous misdirection when the anterior chamber suddenly shallows, particularly after surgery; IOP can remain normal. Choroidal expansion and impaired posterior-to-anterior aqueous movement push the irido-lens diaphragm forward and close the angle. Short axial length, angle-closure and a phakic lens are risk factors. Good preventive and treatment evidence is lacking. Start cycloplegics, specifically atropine or cyclopentolate, with systemic and/or topical aqueous-production suppressants, followed by a hyperosmotic agent such as mannitol when not contraindicated. Ensure a patent peripheral iridotomy. Phakic eyes may require pars plana vitrectomy with or without lens extraction. In pseudophakic eyes, Nd:YAG laser vitreolysis/capsulotomy may be tried. Zonulo-hyaloido-vitrectomy through an anterior-chamber approach using a peripheral iridectomy or iridotomy is an effective option; a pars plana approach is also possible. Diode laser cyclophotocoagulation is an effective alternative in many cases.

document_sections.heading: 4.12 Management differences in small eyes (nanophthalmos)
document_sections.content: The guideline defines nanophthalmos as axial length less than 20.00 mm. Counsel patients that lens or cataract surgery complications may occur in 30% of cases or more, including aqueous misdirection, zonular dialysis, cystoid macular oedema and choroidal effusions (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Strong). Biometry is difficult and potential unexpected refractive outcomes require clear explanation (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Strong). Consider surgical iridectomy during lens extraction to lower postoperative pupil-block risk and facilitate management if aqueous misdirection develops (Evidence/recommendation: Low; Strong). A significant proportion may not attain BCVA > 6/12 after lens or cataract surgery because of amblyopia or foveal hypoplasia (Evidence/recommendation: Low; Weak). For very small eyes with very shallow anterior chambers, consider simultaneous pars plana vitrectomy and phacoemulsification after discussion with a vitreo-retinal surgeon (Evidence/recommendation: Low; Weak).

document_sections.heading: 4.13 Differences in management of four levels of “block”: pupil, ciliary processes/iris crowding, lens (incl. phacomorphic/white cataract) and retrolenticular.
document_sections.content: The site of aqueous-circulation obstruction guides intervention, particularly in atypical presentations. Pupil block and peripheral-iris crowding account for most primary angle-closure; lenticular and retro-lenticular obstruction are considered secondary. Secondary lens-induced disease should be distinguished from ordinary primary disease in which lens size or position makes the anterior chamber shallow: the secondary lens is typically white or unstable. Extraction can be complex and may require mechanical pupil dilation, capsule staining, capsular tension rings or pars planar instruments for a dropped nucleus. Retro-lenticular causes include major vitreous or sub-retinal haemorrhage, inflammatory effusions and tumours. In acute or high-pressure secondary lenticular or retro-lenticular disease, initially dilate with atropine +/- phenylephrine. The treatment distinction is expressed as PRIMARY = PILOCARPINE and SECONDARY = CYCLOPLEGIA.

document_sections.heading: 2. “Atypical disease” – drug induced
document_sections.content: Antidepressant use, including SSRI and tricyclics, is associated with greater angle-closure risk. Inform patients of the excess risk and advise discussion of medication need with the prescribing physician. Idiosyncratic responses to topiramate can cause atypical angle-closure through mechanisms including supraciliary effusions and ciliary rotation. Discuss possible alternative medication with the prescriber.

document_sections.heading: 4.14 Non-penetrating glaucoma surgery and MIGS in angle-closure
document_sections.content: Useful evidence for non-penetrating surgery and MIGS in angle-closure is unavailable. MIGS effectiveness in PACD and PACG remains unproven, and these devices are not licensed for angle-closure in the UK. A meta-analysis of 7 small studies suggested that adding goniosynechialysis (GSL) to phacoemulsification might improve pressure control, but a larger randomised controlled trial found no GSL benefit.

document_sections.heading: 5.1 Benefits and risks
document_sections.content: PACG can produce severe irreversible sight loss and requires careful management. Changes in practice may have unintended consequences. Actively referring and prophylactically treating large numbers of people with narrow angles may be excessively cautious when individual progression risk is low and wider-population risk is falling. Their care uses hospital capacity that could serve other patients. The healthcare slowdown associated with COVID19 in the first 6 months of 2020 intensified the need to weigh benefits, harms and opportunity costs and prioritize people in greatest need. The clinical challenge is identifying those most likely to lose meaningful vision and offering early definitive treatment without treating people unlikely to progress within their lifetime. Recommendations for clear lens extraction in people meeting EAGLE entry criteria do not extend to everyone with narrow angles. Decisions to remove a lens for angle-closure control should involve a consultant with a specialist interest in glaucoma.

document_sections.heading: 5.2 Limitations of the evidence
document_sections.content: Much diagnostic and management evidence comes from East Asia, particularly Singapore, Hong Kong and The Peoples’ Republic of China, where PACG is more common by a factor of 3. UK PACG is less common than POAG and attracts less research priority, although many people are classified as at risk. The guideline therefore draws substantially on studies from other countries. Their East Asian findings provide potentially useful guidance for the UK's multi-ethnic, predominantly white population, especially concerning sight-threatening incident disease among PACS identified during optometric or hospital assessment, but population differences remain relevant to interpretation.

document_sections.heading: 7. Search strategies
document_sections.content: The documented MEDLINE and Embase strategies address angle-closure terminology and classification, UK or comparable-population prevalence and visual morbidity, risk factors, and disease progression or natural history. They combine disease and question-specific search terms with database subject headings and specified exclusions.
